title: 4.10 Module checkpoint
text:
Part A · Which analysis?

Do U19 players improve their 10 m sprint time after 8 weeks of resisted-sprint training? (Same players tested before and after.)

Independent t-test
Paired t-test
Chi-square test


The same players are measured twice: a paired design. See lesson 4.3.



Does the injury rate (injured yes/no) differ between goalkeepers, defenders, midfielders and forwards?

One-way ANOVA
Pearson correlation
Chi-square test of independence


Both variables are categorical, so you compare counts in a 4 × 2 table. See lesson 4.8.



Does VO₂max differ between three groups of runners (sprinters, middle-distance, marathon)?

Three t-tests
One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test
Multiple regression with VO₂max as predictor


3+ groups with a numeric outcome → ANOVA; three separate t-tests inflate the false-positive rate. See lesson 4.4.



Is the relationship between sprint time and jump height still present after accounting for body mass and sex?

Pearson correlation
Multiple regression
Paired t-test


“After accounting for” = adjusting for other variables, which is what multiple regression does. See lesson 4.7.



How consistent is a new jump mat across two trials performed 5 minutes apart?

Independent t-test between trial 1 and trial 2
Typical error / CV, Bland–Altman plot and ICC
Pearson correlation between trial 1 and trial 2 only


Reliability needs absolute (TE, CV, limits of agreement) and relative (ICC) measures. A correlation alone ignores systematic bias. See lesson 4.9.

Question 3: A colleague’s claim
A colleague writes in a draft paper:

“Net propulsive impulse was the strongest determinant of jump height (R² = 0.92, p < 0.001), indicating that coaches should prioritise impulse-oriented training.”



Calculate net_imp = con_impulse_rel − 9.81 × con_time_s and verify the colleague’s R² (r2_net).
Calculate the take-off velocity v_to from jump height and its correlation with net_imp (r_coupling).











squad$con_impulse_rel - 9.81 * squad$con_time_s, sqrt(2 * 9.81 * squad$jump_height_m), cor(squad$net_imp, squad$v_to).




squad$net_imp <- squad$con_impulse_rel - 9.81 * squad$con_time_s
r2_net <- summary(lm(jump_height_m ~ net_imp, data = squad))$r.squared

squad$v_to <- sqrt(2 * 9.81 * squad$jump_height_m)
r_coupling <- cor(squad$net_imp, squad$v_to)

round(c(r2_net = r2_net, r_coupling = r_coupling), 3)
squad$net_imp <- squad$con_impulse_rel - 9.81 * squad$con_time_s
r2_net <- summary(lm(jump_height_m ~ net_imp, data = squad))$r.squared

squad$v_to <- sqrt(2 * 9.81 * squad$jump_height_m)
r_coupling <- cor(squad$net_imp, squad$v_to)

round(c(r2_net = r2_net, r_coupling = r_coupling), 3)







What’s the best revision of the colleague’s sentence?

Report r instead of R²
Use Spearman’s rho because the relationship is non-linear
Remove it as a “finding”: state that net impulse and jump height are mechanically equivalent, and analyse independent determinants (e.g. force–time strategy, depth, body mass) instead


Changing the statistic doesn’t fix mathematical coupling. The analysis has to be redesigned around variables that are not definitions of the outcome. See lesson 4.5.

title: 4.10 Module checkpoint
text:
Congratulations!
You have completed Module 4 · Inferential statistics, and with it the core of this course. You can now import and explore data in R, visualise it to publication standard, and choose, run and critically interpret the most common statistical analyses in sport and exercise science.

title: 4.8 Categorical data: chi-square tests
section: When the outcome is a category
text:
When the outcome is a category
t-tests, ANOVA and regression need a numeric outcome. When both variables are categorical (faller yes/no, injured yes/no, sex, playing position…), you analyse counts in a contingency table instead:








prop.table(tab, margin = 1) divides each row by its total: 25 % of older and 26 % of younger participants reported a fall.

title: 4.8 Categorical data: chi-square tests
section: Goodness-of-fit: does the sample match expected proportions?
text:
Goodness-of-fit: does the sample match expected proportions?
Were men and women recruited equally? H₀: the population proportions are 50 % / 50 %.








The test compares observed counts (116 F, 47 M) with expected counts under H₀ (81.5 each):
\[\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(\text{observed} - \text{expected})^2}{\text{expected}}\]
χ² = 29.2, p < 0.001: women are clearly over-represented in this sample. That’s worth knowing before generalising any result to men!

title: 4.8 Categorical data: chi-square tests
text:
Test of independence
Is falling associated with age group? H₀: the two variables are independent (the proportion of fallers is the same in both age groups).
Under H₀, the expected count in each cell is
\[E = \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{grand total}}\]
and the χ² statistic sums the squared differences between observed and expected counts, as above.

Test whether falling (faller) is associated with age_group.

Make the contingency table tab with table().
Run chisq.test() on it and store the result in res.
Look at the expected counts with res$expected.











table(balance$age_group, balance$faller) and chisq.test(tab).




tab <- table(balance$age_group, balance$faller)
res <- chisq.test(tab)
res
res$expected
tab <- table(balance$age_group, balance$faller)
res <- chisq.test(tab)
res
res$expected












NoteYates’ continuity correction



For 2 × 2 tables, R applies Yates’ correction by default (it says so in the output), which makes the test slightly more conservative. With larger tables, no correction is applied.

title: 4.8 Categorical data: chi-square tests
section: A significant association, and its size
text:
A significant association, and its size
In the squad, are body-mass groups associated with sport?








χ²(2) = 44.9, p < 0.001: a very strong association (we already know basketball players are heavier).
With large samples, even weak associations become significant. Cramér’s V measures the strength of the association on a 0–1 scale:
\[V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{n \times (k - 1)}}\]
where n is the total count and k the smaller of the number of rows and columns. Rough benchmarks for k = 2: 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large.

Calculate Cramér’s V for the association between mass_group and sport. The χ² value is in res$statistic.










V <- sqrt(res$statistic / (n * (k - 1)))




tab2 <- table(squad$mass_group, squad$sport)
res <- chisq.test(tab2)

n <- sum(tab2)
k <- min(nrow(tab2), ncol(tab2))
V <- sqrt(res$statistic / (n * (k - 1)))
unname(V)
tab2 <- table(squad$mass_group, squad$sport)
res <- chisq.test(tab2)

n <- sum(tab2)
k <- min(nrow(tab2), ncol(tab2))
V <- sqrt(res$statistic / (n * (k - 1)))
unname(V)

title: 4.8 Categorical data: chi-square tests
section: Small expected counts: Fisher’s exact test
text:
Small expected counts: Fisher’s exact test
The χ² test is an approximation that works well when all expected counts are at least 5. R warns you when they aren’t. Then use Fisher’s exact test, which calculates the p-value exactly:








For 2 × 2 tables, fisher.test() also gives an odds ratio with its 95 % CI: the odds of being a faller in one group divided by the odds in the other.

Which situation calls for Fisher’s exact test instead of a χ² test?

A 2 × 2 table with 500 participants and all expected counts above 50
A 2 × 2 table of injury (yes/no) by footwear (A/B) in 18 runners, with expected counts of 2 to 7
Comparing mean jump heights between two groups


With small expected counts (< 5), the χ² approximation is unreliable. Means are compared with a t-test, not with a test for counts.



chisq.test(table(balance$fear_falling, balance$faller)) gives p = 0.58. The correct conclusion is:

Fear of falling protects against falls
There is no evidence of an association between the fear-of-falling category and having fallen in this sample
Fallers have more fear of falling


A non-significant result means the data are compatible with independence; it doesn’t prove independence, and the test says nothing about direction.



Why shouldn’t you run a χ² test on a table of percentages?

The test is based on counts; percentages hide the sample size, so χ² would be wrong
Percentages are always below 100
It’s fine as long as they add up to 100 %


χ² depends on the actual numbers: 10 % of 20 athletes and 10 % of 2000 athletes are very different amounts of evidence. Always use the raw counts.

title: 4.6 Simple linear regression
text:
From correlation to regression
Correlation tells you how strongly two variables are related. Regression describes how they’re related: it fits the straight line that best predicts an outcome y from a predictor x:
\[y = b_0 + b_1 x + \varepsilon\]

b₀, the intercept: predicted y when x = 0,
b₁, the slope: the change in y for a 1-unit increase in x,
ε, the residual: the part of y the line doesn’t explain.

“Best” means least squares: the line that minimises the sum of the squared residuals.

title: 4.6 Simple linear regression
text:
Fitting a model with lm()








The formula reads “jump height is modelled by peak power”. The coefficients:

Intercept = −0.018 m: the predicted jump height at 0 W/kg. That’s a meaningless extrapolation far outside the data, and that’s fine: the intercept just anchors the line.
Slope = 0.0076 m per W/kg: each extra 1 W/kg of peak power goes with 0.76 cm more jump height, on average.


The summary() output









Coefficients table: each estimate with its standard error, t value (= estimate / SE) and p-value (H₀: coefficient = 0).
Residual standard error (0.031 m): the typical size of a residual, i.e. how far athletes are from the line, about ±3 cm.
Multiple R-squared (0.69): the proportion of variance in y explained by the model. In simple regression it equals r².
F-statistic: tests the model as a whole (in simple regression, same p as the slope).

Useful extractor functions: coef(model), confint(model) (95 % CIs of the coefficients), summary(model)$r.squared, residuals(model), fitted(model).

Fit a regression predicting jump height from countermovement depth (cmj_depth_m). Store it in model, then extract the slope (slope, the second coefficient) and R² (r2).










lm(jump_height_m ~ cmj_depth_m, data = squad), coef(model)[2], summary(model)$r.squared.




model <- lm(jump_height_m ~ cmj_depth_m, data = squad)
summary(model)

slope <- coef(model)[2]
r2 <- summary(model)$r.squared
model <- lm(jump_height_m ~ cmj_depth_m, data = squad)
summary(model)

slope <- coef(model)[2]
r2 <- summary(model)$r.squared

title: 4.6 Simple linear regression
text:
Predicting
predict() applies the model to new data. Supply a data frame with the predictor column:








The two intervals answer different questions:

confidence interval (39.1–40.4 cm): where is the average jump height of all athletes with 55 W/kg?
prediction interval (33.5–46.0 cm): where will a single new athlete with 55 W/kg probably land? It’s much wider, because it includes the individual scatter around the line.


A coach uses the model to predict the jump height of a 14-year-old with 30 W/kg peak power (the squad ranged from about 40 to 80 W/kg). What’s the problem?

None: the model is significant
The prediction is an extrapolation outside the range of the data, and the youth athlete belongs to a different population
The prediction interval will be too narrow because n is large


Regression models are only trustworthy within the range (and the population) they were fitted on.

title: 4.6 Simple linear regression
text:
Checking the residuals
Linear regression assumes that the residuals:

show no pattern against the fitted values (the relationship is linear),
have roughly constant spread (homoscedasticity),
are roughly normal,
are independent (one observation per athlete).

The quickest check is a plot of residuals against fitted values: you want a shapeless cloud around 0.








(plot(model) in RStudio shows four standard diagnostic plots at once.)

title: 4.6 Simple linear regression
text:
A “perfect” model that explains nothing
Remember mathematical coupling from lesson 4.5? Regression doesn’t protect you from it:








R² = 0.997, a near-perfect model, and completely useless: you can’t “explain” jump height with a variable that was calculated from jump height. A high R² only means something when the predictor is measured independently of the outcome.

A student builds a model predicting jump height from RSImod and is happy with R² = 0.43. What should they consider?

Nothing: 0.43 is a moderate R²
RSImod = jump height / contraction time contains the outcome itself, so part of that R² is built in
They should use a t-test instead


The outcome appears inside the predictor. Part of the “explained” variance is the outcome explaining itself.

title: 4.6 Simple linear regression
text:
Log–log regression and allometric scaling
Many quantities don’t scale 1:1 with body size. Allometry describes this with a power law:
\[Y = a \cdot M^{b}\]
where M is body mass and b the scaling exponent. Taking logarithms turns it into a straight line:
\[\log(Y) = \log(a) + b \cdot \log(M)\]
So a regression of log(Y) on log(M) estimates b as its slope. Dividing by body mass (“per kg” values) silently assumes b = 1. If the true b is smaller, per-kg values will penalise heavier athletes, which is exactly the negative correlation between relative impulse and body mass you saw in lesson 4.5.


Recover the absolute propulsive impulse (N·s) by multiplying con_impulse_rel by body_mass_kg, and store it in squad$impulse.
Fit allo_model: log(impulse) on log(body_mass_kg).
Extract the scaling exponent b (the slope) and its 95 % CI b_ci with confint(). Does the CI include 1?











squad$con_impulse_rel * squad$body_mass_kg, then lm(log(impulse) ~ log(body_mass_kg), data = squad).




# 1. Absolute impulse (N·s)
squad$impulse <- squad$con_impulse_rel * squad$body_mass_kg

# 2. Log-log model
allo_model <- lm(log(impulse) ~ log(body_mass_kg), data = squad)

# 3. Exponent and its CI
b <- coef(allo_model)[2]
b_ci <- confint(allo_model)[2, ]
b
b_ci
# 1. Absolute impulse (N·s)
squad$impulse <- squad$con_impulse_rel * squad$body_mass_kg

# 2. Log-log model
allo_model <- lm(log(impulse) ~ log(body_mass_kg), data = squad)

# 3. Exponent and its CI
b <- coef(allo_model)[2]
b_ci <- confint(allo_model)[2, ]
b
b_ci







In lm(log(Y) ~ log(M)), the slope is 0.67. What happens if you express Y per kg body mass (Y/M)?

Nothing: per-kg values are always size-independent
Heavier athletes get systematically lower per-kg values, because Y grows less than proportionally with M
Lighter athletes get lower per-kg values


Y/M ∝ M0.67−1 = M−0.33, which falls with mass. Divide by M0.67 instead.

title: 4.6 Simple linear regression
text:
Lesson summary

lm(y ~ x, data = df) fits a line; the slope is the change in y per unit of x.
summary() gives coefficients ± SE, p-values, residual SE and R² (= r² in simple regression).
predict(model, newdata, interval = "confidence" / "prediction").
Check residuals vs. fitted values; don’t extrapolate.
A high R² with a coupled predictor is meaningless.
Log–log regression estimates allometric exponents: per-kg values are only fair when b ≈ 1.

title: 4.4 Comparing more than two groups
section: Three groups: light, medium and heavy athletes
text:
Three groups: light, medium and heavy athletes
In the previous lessons, body mass kept appearing as a factor in jump height. To compare three groups, the squad has been split into body-mass tertiles (thirds) with cut() and quantile() (lesson 2.3):

title: 4.4 Comparing more than two groups
text:
Why not three t-tests?
You could compare Light–Medium, Light–Heavy and Medium–Heavy with three t-tests. But each test has a 5 % chance of a false positive, so the chance of at least one false positive across three tests is about \(1 - 0.95^3 = 14\%\). With 5 groups (10 comparisons) it’s 40 %!
ANOVA (analysis of variance) tests all groups at once:

H₀: all population means are equal (μ_Light = μ_Medium = μ_Heavy),
H₁: at least one mean differs.

title: 4.4 Comparing more than two groups
text:
How ANOVA works
ANOVA compares two sources of variability:

between groups: how far the group means are from the overall mean,
within groups: how far the individual athletes are from their own group mean (the “noise”).

The ratio is the F-statistic:
\[F = \frac{\text{variance between groups}}{\text{variance within groups}}\]
If H₀ is true, the group means differ only by chance and F ≈ 1. A large F means the groups differ more than chance would explain.

title: 4.4 Comparing more than two groups
text:
One-way ANOVA in R
Fit the model with aov(outcome ~ group, data = ...) and show the ANOVA table with summary():








The table shows, for the groups (mass_group) and the residual (within-group) variation: degrees of freedom (Df), sums of squares (Sum Sq), mean squares (Mean Sq = Sum Sq / Df), the F value (= Mean Sq groups / Mean Sq residuals) and the p-value.
Here F(2, 81) = 4.70, p = 0.012: the mean jump height differs between the body-mass groups.

Using the balance data, test whether the Mini-BESTest score (minibest) differs between the three physical-activity levels (activity). Fit the ANOVA (model) and show the table.










aov(minibest ~ activity, data = balance)




model <- aov(minibest ~ activity, data = balance)
summary(model)
model <- aov(minibest ~ activity, data = balance)
summary(model)

title: 4.4 Comparing more than two groups
text:
Post-hoc tests: which groups differ?
A significant ANOVA says some means differ, not which. Post-hoc tests compare all pairs while controlling the overall false-positive rate. Tukey’s HSD (honestly significant difference) is the standard choice:








For each pair you get the difference (diff), its adjusted 95 % CI (lwr, upr) and the adjusted p-value (p adj). Only Heavy vs. Light is significant (−4.2 cm, p = 0.013); Heavy vs. Medium is borderline (p = 0.06).

An ANOVA comparing four training groups gives p = 0.003. What can you conclude?

All four groups differ from each other
At least one group mean differs from the others; a post-hoc test is needed to find which
The first group is the best


The ANOVA’s H₁ is “not all means are equal”. Use Tukey’s HSD (or planned comparisons) to locate the differences.

title: 4.4 Comparing more than two groups
text:
Effect size: η² (eta squared)
The p-value doesn’t say how important the group differences are. η² is the proportion of the total variability in the outcome explained by the groups:
\[\eta^2 = \frac{SS_{between}}{SS_{total}} = \frac{SS_{between}}{SS_{between} + SS_{within}}\]
Rough benchmarks: 0.01 small, 0.06 medium, 0.14 large.

Calculate η² for the body-mass ANOVA. The sums of squares are in the ANOVA table: summary(model)[[1]]$"Sum Sq" gives a vector with SS_between (first) and SS_within (second).










eta_sq <- ss[1] / sum(ss)




model <- aov(jump_height_m ~ mass_group, data = squad)
ss <- summary(model)[[1]]$"Sum Sq"
ss

eta_sq <- ss[1] / sum(ss)
eta_sq
model <- aov(jump_height_m ~ mass_group, data = squad)
ss <- summary(model)[[1]]$"Sum Sq"
ss

eta_sq <- ss[1] / sum(ss)
eta_sq

title: 4.4 Comparing more than two groups
text:
Assumptions
One-way ANOVA assumes:

independent observations,
roughly normal residuals in each group,
equal variances across groups (homogeneity of variance).

Check the residuals visually, and compare the group SDs. A common rule of thumb: the largest SD shouldn’t be more than about twice the smallest.








If the assumptions are badly violated:

unequal variances → Welch’s ANOVA: oneway.test(y ~ group, data = ...),
non-normal / ordinal data → Kruskal–Wallis test: kruskal.test(y ~ group, data = ...).










What does TukeyHSD() do that three separate t-tests don’t?

It uses the median instead of the mean
It adjusts the p-values and CIs for the number of comparisons, keeping the overall false-positive rate at 5 %
It works without a significant ANOVA


Without adjustment, the family-wise error rate grows with every extra comparison. Tukey’s method controls it.



You compare the sprint times of two groups with an ANOVA instead of a t-test. What happens?

You get an error
You get the same p-value as a Student t-test (F = t²)
The result is always more significant


With two groups, one-way ANOVA and the equal-variance t-test are mathematically identical. ANOVA is the generalisation to more groups.

title: 4.4 Comparing more than two groups
text:
Lesson summary

3+ groups: one-way ANOVA, summary(aov(y ~ group, data = df)). Report F(df₁, df₂) and p.
F = between-group variance / within-group variance.
Follow a significant ANOVA with TukeyHSD(model).
Effect size η² = SS_between / SS_total.
Alternatives: oneway.test() (unequal variances), kruskal.test() (non-parametric).


Scratchpad
squad (with mass_group) and balance are loaded.

title: 4.2 Hypothesis testing
section: The logic of a hypothesis test
text:
The logic of a hypothesis test
A strength coach claims: “Professional athletes in our league jump 40 cm on average.” Our squad of 84 athletes has a mean of:








That’s 39.3 cm, not 40 cm. But samples always differ a bit from the population. Is this difference larger than what sampling variability alone would produce? A hypothesis test answers this in four steps:

State the hypotheses.

Null hypothesis H₀: nothing special is going on. The population mean is 0.40 m.
Alternative hypothesis H₁: the population mean is not 0.40 m.

Calculate a test statistic that measures how far the data are from H₀, in units of standard error. For a mean, that’s the t-statistic: \[t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{SE}\]
Find the p-value: the probability of getting a t at least this extreme if H₀ were true.
Decide: if p is smaller than a pre-chosen significance level α (usually 0.05), reject H₀ (“statistically significant”). Otherwise, you fail to reject H₀.

title: 4.2 Hypothesis testing
text:
The one-sample t-test
t.test(x, mu = value) tests whether the mean of x differs from value:








The output gives the t-statistic, the degrees of freedom (n − 1), the p-value, the 95 % CI and the sample mean. Here p ≈ 0.29 > 0.05, so we cannot reject the coach’s claim. A 0.7 cm difference is easily explained by sampling variability.
Notice that 0.40 m lies inside the 95 % CI. That’s no coincidence: a two-sided test at α = 0.05 is significant exactly when the hypothesised value lies outside the 95 % CI.

A physiotherapist states that the average mean propulsive force (con_force_rel) of professional athletes is 20 N/kg. Test this claim with a one-sample t-test on the squad data. Store the result in res, then print the p-value with res$p.value.










t.test(squad$con_force_rel, mu = 20)




res <- t.test(squad$con_force_rel, mu = 20)
res
res$p.value
res <- t.test(squad$con_force_rel, mu = 20)
res
res$p.value

title: 4.2 Hypothesis testing
section: What a p-value is, and what it isn’t
text:
What a p-value is, and what it isn’t
The p-value is: the probability of observing data at least as extreme as ours, assuming H₀ is true.
A small p means the data would be surprising if H₀ were true. Common misinterpretations:







❌ Wrong
✅ Why




“p = 0.03 means there’s a 3 % chance H₀ is true.”
p is calculated assuming H₀ is true; it can’t be the probability of H₀.


“p > 0.05 proves there’s no effect.”
Absence of evidence isn’t evidence of absence. The study may simply be too small.


“A smaller p means a bigger effect.”
p depends on effect size and sample size. A tiny effect in a huge sample can give a tiny p.


“p < 0.05 means the result is important.”
Statistical significance ≠ practical importance (see below).




A study finds p = 0.20 for the difference in sprint time between two training groups. What can you conclude?

The two training methods are equally effective
The data don’t provide convincing evidence of a difference; a real difference could still exist
There is a 20 % chance that the training methods differ


Failing to reject H₀ isn’t proof of H₀. Look at the CI of the difference: if it’s wide, the study is inconclusive.

title: 4.2 Hypothesis testing
text:
Two kinds of errors
Every decision can be wrong in two ways:









H₀ is actually true
H₀ is actually false




Reject H₀
❌ Type I error (false positive), probability α
✅ correct (probability = power)


Don’t reject H₀
✅ correct
❌ Type II error (false negative), probability β



α is the risk you accept of declaring an effect that doesn’t exist. With α = 0.05, 1 in 20 tests of a true null hypothesis will be “significant” by chance. Let’s check that with a simulation: two groups drawn from the same population, so H₀ is true:








About 5 % false positives, as promised. Now imagine a study measuring 20 different variables, each tested at α = 0.05: you’d expect one “significant” result even if nothing is going on. This is the multiple comparisons problem, and it’s why fishing through many variables for p < 0.05 is bad practice.

title: 4.2 Hypothesis testing
text:
Statistical power
Power (1 − β) is the probability that a test detects an effect that really exists. It depends on:

the effect size (bigger effects are easier to detect),
the sample size (more athletes → more power),
the variability of the measurements (a more reliable test → more power),
α.

Studies in sport science often have small samples and therefore low power: they may miss real effects, and the significant effects they do find tend to be overestimated.

Estimate power by simulation. Suppose a training programme truly improves jump height by 3 cm (from 40 to 43 cm, SD 5 cm). With 20 athletes per group, how often would a t-test detect it?
Complete the code: the second group’s mean should be 43. power_20 is the proportion of the 1000 simulated studies with p < 0.05.










mean = 43 and power_20 <- mean(p_values < 0.05).




set.seed(42)
p_values <- replicate(1000, t.test(rnorm(20, mean = 40, sd = 5),
                                   rnorm(20, mean = 43, sd = 5))$p.value)
power_20 <- mean(p_values < 0.05)
power_20
set.seed(42)
p_values <- replicate(1000, t.test(rnorm(20, mean = 40, sd = 5),
                                   rnorm(20, mean = 43, sd = 5))$p.value)
power_20 <- mean(p_values < 0.05)
power_20







A study with 8 athletes per group finds no significant effect of a supplement (p = 0.31). What’s the most likely issue?

The supplement has no effect
The study may have had too little power to detect a realistic effect
α was set too low


With 8 per group, only large effects can be detected reliably. Report the effect size with its CI, and plan sample sizes with a power analysis before collecting data.

title: 4.2 Hypothesis testing
text:
Statistical vs. practical significance
With enough data, any tiny difference becomes “statistically significant”. The question a coach cares about is: is the difference big enough to matter?
Imagine 5,000 athletes per group with a true difference of 0.3 cm in jump height:








p is small, but 0.3 cm is less than the trial-to-trial variation of a single athlete. It’s practically irrelevant. Always report and interpret:

the effect size in meaningful units (cm, %, s) or as a standardised effect (Cohen’s d, lesson 4.3),
its confidence interval,
whether it exceeds the smallest worthwhile change for your context (lesson 4.9).


A large study reports that a new shoe improves sprint time by 0.004 s over 30 m (p = 0.001). The best summary is:

The shoe makes athletes much faster
The effect is statistically significant, but probably too small to matter in practice
The result must be a type I error


A p-value says nothing about the size of the effect. 4 milliseconds over 30 m is smaller than the timing gates’ precision.

title: 4.2 Hypothesis testing
text:
Lesson summary

Hypothesis test: H₀ vs. H₁ → test statistic → p-value → compare with α.
t.test(x, mu = value): one-sample t-test. Results: $statistic, $p.value, $conf.int, $estimate.
p = P(data this extreme | H₀ true). It’s not the probability that H₀ is true, and not a measure of effect size.
Type I error = false positive (α); type II error = false negative (β); power = 1 − β.
Report effect sizes with CIs and judge practical relevance, not just p < 0.05.

title: 3.6 Module checkpoint
text:
Part A · Quick quiz

Which code shows the raw data and the mean ± SD per group?

geom_col() + geom_errorbar()
geom_jitter() + stat_summary(fun = mean, fun.min = ..., fun.max = ..., geom = "pointrange")
geom_boxplot()


The jittered points show each athlete; stat_summary() adds the mean ± SD on top. A box plot shows median and quartiles, not mean ± SD. See lesson 3.1.



You want one panel per sport, with the panels stacked vertically. Which code?

facet_grid(sport ~ sport)
facet_wrap(~ sport, ncol = 1)
facet_wrap(sport)


facet_wrap(~ sport, ncol = 1). The ~ is required, and ncol = 1 stacks the panels. See lesson 3.2.



You zoom a box plot with scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.3, 0.5)) and get a warning: “Removed 6 rows containing non-finite values”. What happened?

Nothing important: the warning can be ignored
The 6 values outside the limits were removed before the boxes were calculated, so the boxes are now wrong
6 values were missing in the original data


limits deletes data. Use coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.3, 0.5)) to zoom without changing the statistics. See lesson 3.3.



p + theme(legend.position = "top") + theme_classic(): where is the legend?

At the top
On the right (the default), because theme_classic() reset it
Nowhere


Complete themes override earlier theme() settings. Add them first. See lesson 3.4.



In patchwork, what does p1 / p2 do?

Divides the values of p1 by p2
Places p1 above p2
Places p1 next to p2


/ stacks plots vertically, | places them side by side. See lesson 3.5.

title: 3.6 Module checkpoint
section: Part B · A figure that checks the physics
text:
Part B · A figure that checks the physics
Physics gives us two ways to look at the velocity of an athlete’s centre of mass:

The take-off velocity follows from the jump height: a body that rises h metres must leave the ground with \(v_{TO} = \sqrt{2 g h}\).
The force platform also records the peak velocity (peak_velocity) during push-off. Peak velocity is reached just before take-off, because in the last milliseconds the force drops below body weight and the athlete already starts to slow down.

So we expect: peak velocity ≥ take-off velocity, for every athlete. A good figure can check this.

Step 1 · Panel A: jump height by sport

Create pA: jump height in cm by sport, showing

the raw data: geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, aes(colour = sport), show.legend = FALSE),
the mean ± SD in black: stat_summary() with geom = "pointrange",
colours from sport_cols with scale_colour_manual(),
labels x = NULL, y = "Jump height (cm)", and theme_classic(base_size = 14).











geom = "pointrange", values = sport_cols, y = "Jump height (cm)".




pA <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m * 100)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, aes(colour = sport), show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean,
               fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x),
               fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x),
               geom = "pointrange", size = 0.8, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Jump height (cm)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
pA
pA <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m * 100)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, aes(colour = sport), show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean,
               fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x),
               fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x),
               geom = "pointrange", size = 0.8, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Jump height (cm)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
pA








Step 2 · Panel B: peak vs. take-off velocity


Add a column v_to to squad: the take-off velocity, sqrt(2 * 9.81 * jump_height_m).
Create pB: a scatter plot of v_to (x) against peak_velocity (y), coloured by sport (with sport_cols), with the identity line geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed").
Find the athlete(s) whose peak velocity is lower than their take-off velocity and store them in suspect.












sqrt(2 * 9.81 * squad$jump_height_m)
intercept = 0, slope = 1
subset(squad, peak_velocity < v_to)





# 1. Take-off velocity from jump height
squad$v_to <- sqrt(2 * 9.81 * squad$jump_height_m)

# 2. Peak vs. take-off velocity
pB <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = v_to, y = peak_velocity, colour = sport)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Take-off velocity (m/s)", y = "Peak velocity (m/s)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
pB

# 3. Athletes that break the physics
suspect <- subset(squad, peak_velocity < v_to)
suspect[, c("id", "v_to", "peak_velocity")]
# 1. Take-off velocity from jump height
squad$v_to <- sqrt(2 * 9.81 * squad$jump_height_m)

# 2. Peak vs. take-off velocity
pB <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = v_to, y = peak_velocity, colour = sport)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Take-off velocity (m/s)", y = "Peak velocity (m/s)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
pB

# 3. Athletes that break the physics
suspect <- subset(squad, peak_velocity < v_to)
suspect[, c("id", "v_to", "peak_velocity")]








Step 3 · Combine the panels

Recreate pA and pB (given) and combine them side by side with panel tags A and B.










(pA | pB) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")




squad$v_to <- sqrt(2 * 9.81 * squad$jump_height_m)
pA <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m * 100)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, aes(colour = sport), show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x), fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x),
               geom = "pointrange", size = 0.8, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Jump height (cm)") + theme_classic(base_size = 14)
pB <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = v_to, y = peak_velocity, colour = sport)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Take-off velocity (m/s)", y = "Peak velocity (m/s)", colour = NULL) + theme_classic(base_size = 14)

# Combine side by side with tags A and B
(pA | pB) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
squad$v_to <- sqrt(2 * 9.81 * squad$jump_height_m)
pA <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m * 100)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, aes(colour = sport), show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x), fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x),
               geom = "pointrange", size = 0.8, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Jump height (cm)") + theme_classic(base_size = 14)
pB <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = v_to, y = peak_velocity, colour = sport)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") + geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Take-off velocity (m/s)", y = "Peak velocity (m/s)", colour = NULL) + theme_classic(base_size = 14)

# Combine side by side with tags A and B
(pA | pB) + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

title: 3.4 Themes and publication-ready figures
text:
Complete themes
A theme controls everything that is not data: background, grid lines, fonts, legend position, axis lines. ggplot2’s default is theme_gray(). Other complete themes:








Notice that a plot can be stored in a variable (p) and extended later with +. That’s very handy for trying out styles.
theme_classic() (white background, axis lines, no grid) is the style most often seen in sport-science journals.
All complete themes have a base_size argument that scales all text. The default (11 pt) is often too small, especially for slides:

title: 3.4 Themes and publication-ready figures
text:
Fine-tuning with theme()
Add theme() after the complete theme to change individual elements. Each element is set with a matching element_*() function:








Element type
Function
Examples




text
element_text(size, face, colour, angle)
axis.title, axis.text, plot.title, legend.text


lines
element_line(colour, linewidth, linetype)
axis.line, panel.grid.major


boxes
element_rect(fill, colour)
panel.background, legend.background


remove
element_blank()
anything you want to hide



Plus some non-element settings, e.g. legend.position = "top" / "bottom" / "none" / c(0.8, 0.9) (inside the panel).









Starting from p (given), add theme_classic(base_size = 14) and then a theme() call that:

moves the legend to the bottom,
makes the axis titles bold (face = "bold").











base_size = 14, legend.position = "bottom", face = "bold".




p <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg, y = jump_height_m, colour = sport)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Jump height (m)", colour = NULL)

p + theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
p <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg, y = jump_height_m, colour = sport)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Jump height (m)", colour = NULL)

p + theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )







You write p + theme(legend.position = "none") + theme_classic(). The legend is still there. Why?

legend.position doesn’t exist
A complete theme added afterwards overrides all earlier theme settings
You need element_blank() to remove a legend


Order matters: complete themes reset everything. Always add the complete theme first, then your theme() tweaks.

title: 3.4 Themes and publication-ready figures
text:
Your own reusable theme
For a report or thesis, all figures should look the same. Instead of copying the same theme() code into every plot, store it once:








This creates a function theme_lab() that you can add to any plot:








You can also make it the default for every plot in a script with theme_set(theme_lab()). (guide = "none" in a scale hides that legend.)

title: 3.4 Themes and publication-ready figures
text:
Exporting figures with ggsave()
A figure for a journal or thesis must be saved at the right size and resolution. Don’t copy it from the RStudio Viewer: use ggsave().
my_plot <- ggplot(...) + ...

ggsave("figure1.png", plot = my_plot, width = 17, height = 10, units = "cm", dpi = 300)
ggsave("figure1.pdf", plot = my_plot, width = 17, height = 10, units = "cm")
ggsave("figure1.tiff", plot = my_plot, width = 8.5, height = 7, units = "cm", dpi = 600)







Setting
Typical journal requirement




Width
single column ≈ 8–9 cm, double column ≈ 17–18 cm


Resolution (dpi)
≥ 300 dpi for photos/plots, 600–1000 for line art


Format
PDF/EPS/SVG (vector, sharp at any zoom) or high-res TIFF/PNG









TipSize first, then fonts



Text in a figure saved at 8.5 cm wide will look much bigger than in the same figure saved at 30 cm, because base_size is in points and doesn’t scale with the figure. Decide the final width first, save it, and check that the smallest text is still ≥ 7–8 pt at print size.


ggsave() runs here in the browser too, but the file is stored in the browser’s temporary file system, so you can’t open it. Try it in RStudio, where the file appears in your project folder.

Which format keeps a plot perfectly sharp at any zoom level?

PNG at 72 dpi
JPEG
PDF or SVG (vector formats)


Vector formats store shapes and text, not pixels, so they never get blurry. JPEG also adds compression artefacts around text and lines, so avoid it for plots.



Write a theme function theme_poster() for a conference poster. It should:

start from theme_bw() with a base_size of 20,
remove the minor grid lines (panel.grid.minor = element_blank()).

Then apply it to the plot on the last line.










base_size = 20, panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), and add theme_poster() to the plot.




theme_poster <- function() {
  theme_bw(base_size = 20) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_poster()
theme_poster <- function() {
  theme_bw(base_size = 20) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_poster()

title: 3.4 Themes and publication-ready figures
text:
A checklist for publication-quality figures
Before you submit a figure, check that:

every axis has a title with units,
text is large enough at the final printed size,
colours are colour-blind friendly and still distinguishable in grey-scale,
the raw data are visible where possible, not just means,
the caption says what error bars show (SD, SE or CI) and how many observations there are,
axis limits don’t exaggerate differences (bar charts must start at 0),
there’s no chart junk: unnecessary 3D effects, shading, heavy grids or redundant legends,
all figures share a consistent style (same theme, same colour for the same group),
it’s saved with ggsave() at the required size, resolution and format.


A bar chart of mean jump heights (38 vs. 41 cm) has a y-axis starting at 37 cm, making one bar look three times taller than the other. What’s the problem?

Nothing: zooming makes differences visible
Bars encode values by their length from zero, so a truncated axis exaggerates the difference
The bars should be horizontal


For bar charts the length of the bar is the value, so the axis must start at 0. If you need to zoom, use points (e.g. mean ± SD with the raw data) instead of bars.

title: 3.4 Themes and publication-ready figures
text:
Lesson summary

Complete themes (theme_classic(), theme_bw(), …) set the overall look; base_size scales the text.
theme() + element_text() / element_line() / element_rect() / element_blank() fine-tune elements. Add it after the complete theme.
Store your style in a function (theme_lab <- function() theme_classic() + theme(...)) and reuse it.
Export with ggsave(file, plot, width, height, units = "cm", dpi = 300); prefer vector formats.


Scratchpad

title: 3.2 Facets, reference lines and annotations
text:
Small multiples with facet_wrap()
A facet splits one plot into several panels, one per group, all with the same axes. This is often clearer than squeezing every group into one panel with different colours. facet_wrap(~ variable) creates one panel per value of variable:








Useful arguments:

ncol / nrow: the layout of the panels,
scales = "free_y" (or "free_x", "free"): let each panel have its own axis range. Use this with care, because readers naturally compare panels as if the axes were the same!


Make histograms of body_mass_kg (binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white"), with one panel per sport stacked vertically (ncol = 1), so the two distributions are easy to compare on the same x-axis.










facet_wrap(~ sport, ncol = 1). Don’t forget the tilde ~.




ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ sport, ncol = 1)
ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ sport, ncol = 1)

title: 3.2 Facets, reference lines and annotations
text:
Two-way grids with facet_grid()
facet_grid(rows ~ cols) makes a grid with one variable defining the rows and another the columns:








Use . for “no variable”: facet_grid(. ~ sex) gives one row of panels.

You use facet_wrap(~ sport, scales = "free_y"). What’s the risk?

The plot becomes slower
Each panel gets its own y-range, so readers may misjudge differences between panels
Points are removed from the plot


Free scales are useful when groups have very different ranges, but the same visual height then means different values in different panels. Mention it in the caption, or keep the scales fixed when comparing groups is the point of the figure.

title: 3.2 Facets, reference lines and annotations
text:
More variables: shape and size
Besides x, y, colour and fill, points have a shape (good for a categorical variable, especially in black-and-white print) and a size (for a numeric variable, a “bubble chart”):








This one plot shows four variables. Notice the pattern: for the same jump height (colour), athletes with a shorter push-off (x) produce a larger force (y). Keep this in mind for the regression lesson in Module 4!






Warning



Don’t overdo it. Four variables in one plot is usually the maximum readers can digest. If it gets crowded, use facets instead.

title: 3.2 Facets, reference lines and annotations
text:
Reference lines
Reference lines give the reader a benchmark:

geom_hline(yintercept = ...): a horizontal line, e.g. a target value or a group mean,
geom_vline(xintercept = ...): a vertical line,
geom_abline(intercept = ..., slope = ...): any straight line. With intercept 0 and slope 1 it’s the identity line (y = x).










Catching a data error with an identity line
The dataset contains the peak (ecc_rfd_max) and the mean (ecc_rfd_mean) eccentric rate of force development of every athlete. By definition, the peak of a signal can never be smaller than its mean. Plot them against each other with the identity line y = x: every point must lie on the side of the line where max > mean.

Make a scatter plot of ecc_rfd_mean (x) against ecc_rfd_max (y) and add the identity line with geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed"). Then, on the last line of code, use subset() to find the athlete(s) whose max is smaller than their mean.










intercept = 0, slope = 1, and subset(squad, ecc_rfd_max < ecc_rfd_mean).




p <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = ecc_rfd_mean, y = ecc_rfd_max)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed")
print(p)

# Which athlete(s) have max < mean?
subset(squad, ecc_rfd_max < ecc_rfd_mean)[, c("id", "ecc_rfd_mean", "ecc_rfd_max")]
p <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = ecc_rfd_mean, y = ecc_rfd_max)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed")
print(p)

# Which athlete(s) have max < mean?
subset(squad, ecc_rfd_max < ecc_rfd_mean)[, c("id", "ecc_rfd_mean", "ecc_rfd_max")]

title: 3.2 Facets, reference lines and annotations
text:
Annotations
Use annotate() to add text, arrows or shaded areas at specific coordinates. These are not mapped from the data:









Labelling individual points
To label points with a value from the data (e.g. athlete IDs), use geom_text() with the label aesthetic. When labels overlap, the ggrepel package’s geom_text_repel() pushes them apart. Labelling every point is cluttered, so pass a subset of the data to the label layer:








Each layer can use its own data via the data argument, which is very handy for highlighting.

Highlight and label the five athletes with the shortest contraction time (contraction_time_s) in a scatter plot of contraction_time_s (x) against jump_height_m (y).

fast (the five fastest athletes) is created for you with order() and head().
Add a red point layer and a geom_text_repel() layer that both use data = fast.











Use data = fast in both layers and aes(label = id).




fast <- head(squad[order(squad$contraction_time_s), ], 5)

ggplot(squad, aes(x = contraction_time_s, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = fast, colour = "red", size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(data = fast, aes(label = id), colour = "red")
fast <- head(squad[order(squad$contraction_time_s), ], 5)

ggplot(squad, aes(x = contraction_time_s, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(data = fast, colour = "red", size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(data = fast, aes(label = id), colour = "red")







Which function draws the line y = x?

geom_hline(yintercept = 1)
geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1)
geom_vline(xintercept = 0)


geom_abline() draws a line with a given intercept and slope. Intercept 0 and slope 1 is the identity line, ideal for comparing two measurements of the same quantity (e.g. two devices, or test vs. retest).



In geom_point(data = top, colour = "red"), what does data = top do?

It replaces the data for the whole plot
Only this layer uses the data frame top; the other layers keep the main data
It gives an error, because data can only be set in ggplot()


Every layer can have its own data. This is how you highlight or label a subset of observations.

title: 3.2 Facets, reference lines and annotations
text:
Lesson summary

facet_wrap(~ var) → panels per group; facet_grid(rows ~ cols) → a grid; scales = "free" with care.
shape (categorical) and size (numeric) add variables, but don’t overload a plot.
Reference lines: geom_hline(), geom_vline(), geom_abline(); an identity line is great for spotting impossible values.
annotate() adds fixed text and shapes; geom_text_repel(data = subset, aes(label = ...)) labels selected points.


Scratchpad
squad and balance are loaded, along with ggrepel.

title: 2.5 Module checkpoint
text:
Part A · Quick quiz

A study reports “Mean age 24.3 ± 3.1 years (mean ± SD) of the 18 participants”. This is…

descriptive statistics
inferential statistics


It summarises the sample without generalising to a population. See lesson 2.1.



Training load measured as session-RPE (RPE × duration in minutes), e.g. 420 AU, is best treated as…

numerical (continuous)
nominal
ordinal


Although RPE itself is a rating, session-RPE is a product with many possible values and is analysed as a numerical variable in practice.



Ground contact times of a sprinter (ms): 98, 101, 97, 99, 180. The 180 ms value came from a stumble. Which summary describes the typical contact time best?

Mean
Median
Range


The median (99 ms) ignores the extreme value; the mean (115 ms) is pulled up by the stumble. See lesson 2.2.



Squad A has a mean CMJ of 40 cm (SD 2 cm), squad B 40 cm (SD 6 cm). Which statement is correct?

Squad B jumps higher
Jump heights vary much more between players in squad B
Squad A has more outliers


Same center, different spread. See lesson 2.3.



For a variable, Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 18. Is a value of 26 an outlier according to the IQR rule?

Yes
No


IQR = 18 − 12 = 6, so the upper fence is 18 + 1.5 × 6 = 27. A value of 26 is below the fence, so it is not flagged (although it is close). See lesson 2.3.



According to the central limit theorem, the standard error of a mean based on 9 trials is…

the SD of single trials divided by 9
the SD of single trials divided by 3
the same as the SD of single trials


SE = SD / √n = SD / √9 = SD / 3. See lesson 2.4.

text:
Part B · From raw force to jump height
Athlete K’s three CMJs are loaded in cmj (columns trial, time_s, force_left, force_right, force_total; 500 samples per second). Here are all three:








(facet_wrap(~ trial) draws one panel per trial. You’ll learn more about facets in Module 3.)

Step 1 · Body weight and data quality
Before analysing a jump you need the athlete’s body weight, from a stable quiet-standing phase. Look at the plot: CMJ 1 and CMJ 3 start with a long, flat phase, but CMJ 2 starts while the athlete is still settling on the plate.


Create quiet1: rows of cmj for CMJ 1 with time_s <= 2.
Create quiet2: rows of cmj for CMJ 2 with time_s <= 1 (its only “quiet” part).
Calculate the SD of force_total for each, and store them in sd1 and sd2.
On the last line, calculate how many times larger sd2 is than sd1.











Combine conditions with &: subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 2" & time_s <= 1). Then sd(quiet1$force_total) and sd2 / sd1.




# 1 and 2. Quiet-standing phases
quiet1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1" & time_s <= 2)
quiet2 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 2" & time_s <= 1)

# 3. SD of the force during quiet standing
sd1 <- sd(quiet1$force_total)
sd2 <- sd(quiet2$force_total)

# 4. How many times noisier is CMJ 2?
sd2 / sd1
# 1 and 2. Quiet-standing phases
quiet1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1" & time_s <= 2)
quiet2 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 2" & time_s <= 1)

# 3. SD of the force during quiet standing
sd1 <- sd(quiet1$force_total)
sd2 <- sd(quiet2$force_total)

# 4. How many times noisier is CMJ 2?
sd2 / sd1








Step 2 · Flight time and jump height
During flight the force is (almost) zero. The flight time is the number of samples below a small threshold (we’ll use 20 N) multiplied by the time between samples (0.002 s). From the flight time t, physics gives the jump height:
\[h = \frac{g \, t^2}{8}, \qquad g = 9.81 \text{ m/s}^2\]

For CMJ 1:

Create cmj1, the rows of cmj for CMJ 1.
Calculate flight_time (s): the number of samples with force_total < 20, times 0.002. Tip: sum() of a logical vector counts the TRUEs.
Calculate height_cm, the jump height in cm (the formula gives metres, so multiply by 100).












sum(cmj1$force_total < 20) * 0.002
9.81 * flight_time^2 / 8 * 100





# 1. Data of CMJ 1
cmj1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1")

# 2. Flight time (s)
flight_time <- sum(cmj1$force_total < 20) * 0.002

# 3. Jump height (cm)
height_cm <- 9.81 * flight_time^2 / 8 * 100

flight_time
height_cm

flight_time
height_cm








Step 3 · Summarise the three jumps
Now do it for all three trials at once. tapply() (from lesson 2.2) applies a function per trial.


flight is calculated for you for each trial. Calculate the jump heights (cm) for all three trials, using the vector flight.
Calculate the mean (mean_h), standard deviation (sd_h) and coefficient of variation in % (cv_h) of the three heights.












Arithmetic works on whole vectors: 9.81 * flight^2 / 8 * 100
mean(heights), sd(heights), sd_h / mean_h * 100





# Flight time per trial (s)
flight <- tapply(cmj$force_total < 20, cmj$trial, sum) * 0.002
flight

# 1. Jump heights (cm)

# 2. Mean, SD and CV
mean_h <- mean(heights)

round(heights, 1)

Step 4 · Left vs. right
A dual force platform also lets you compare the legs. During quiet standing, a healthy athlete usually carries roughly half their weight on each leg.

Using quiet1 (quiet standing in CMJ 1, given), calculate the median force under the left and the right foot (left_med, right_med). Then calculate the percentage of body weight on the left leg: left_med / (left_med + right_med) * 100.










median(quiet1$force_left), median(quiet1$force_right), then left_med / (left_med + right_med) * 100.

right_med <- median(quiet1$force_right)

# Percentage of weight on the left leg

title: 2.5 Module checkpoint
text:
Well done!
You’ve completed Module 2 · Introduction to statistics. You can now describe data with measures of center and spread, recognise normal data, and explain the central limit theorem: everything you need to start with inferential statistics.

Scratchpad

title: 2.3 Measures of spread
text:
Measures of spread
Two athletes each perform five CMJs:








Both have a mean of exactly 40 cm, but they are clearly not the same: A is very consistent, B is all over the place. A measure of center alone hides this. A measure of spread (or variability, dispersion) describes how far the values are scattered around the center.
The simplest is the range: maximum minus minimum.








The range is easy to understand, but it depends on only two values (the most extreme ones), so a single unusual trial changes it completely. We need measures that use all the data.

title: 2.3 Measures of spread
text:
Variance and standard deviation
The idea: measure how far each value is from the mean (its deviation), and average those distances.
Let’s do it step by step for athlete B:








Because the deviations always sum to zero, we square them first (squares are always positive). The average squared deviation is the variance:
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\]
Because the deviations were squared, the variance is in squared units (cm²), which is hard to interpret. Taking the square root brings us back to the original units. This is the standard deviation (SD):
\[s = \sqrt{s^2}\]








R does all of this for you with var() and sd():








Athlete B’s SD (7.9 cm) is more than 10 times larger than athlete A’s (0.7 cm). Roughly speaking, the SD is the typical distance of a value from the mean.






TipWhy divide by n − 1?



We usually calculate the SD of a sample to estimate the spread in the population. Deviations are measured from the sample mean, which is always a bit closer to the sample values than the unknown population mean. Dividing by n − 1 instead of n corrects for this. R’s var() and sd() always use n − 1.



Calculate the variance of sprint by hand, following the steps above, and store it in var_by_hand. Then calculate the standard deviation with sd() and store it in sd_sprint.










sum(dev^2) / (length(sprint) - 1), and sd(sprint). Check that var_by_hand equals var(sprint).




sprint <- c(4.12, 4.05, 4.20, 3.98, 4.15)   # 30 m sprint times (s)

# Variance by hand
dev <- sprint - mean(sprint)
var_by_hand <- sum(dev^2) / (length(sprint) - 1)

# Standard deviation
sd_sprint <- sd(sprint)

var_by_hand
sd_sprint
sprint <- c(4.12, 4.05, 4.20, 3.98, 4.15)   # 30 m sprint times (s)

# Variance by hand
dev <- sprint - mean(sprint)
var_by_hand <- sum(dev^2) / (length(sprint) - 1)

# Standard deviation
sd_sprint <- sd(sprint)

var_by_hand
sd_sprint







Using the SD on force data: when does the jump start?
When analysing a CMJ, you need to know when the movement starts. During quiet standing the force wobbles randomly around body weight. A common rule (e.g. Owen et al., 2014) is: the movement starts when the force drops more than 5 SDs below body weight. A drop that big is very unlikely to be just noise.
The quiet-standing data of CMJ 3 is loaded as quiet (0–1.5 s).


Calculate body weight (bw, the mean of quiet$force_total) and the SD of the quiet-standing force (bw_sd).
Calculate the onset threshold = bw - 5 * bw_sd.
Find the first time at which cmj3$force_total drops below the threshold. which() returns the positions where a condition is TRUE, and [1] takes the first one. This is given for you.











mean(quiet$force_total), sd(quiet$force_total), and bw - 5 * bw_sd.




# 1. Body weight and its SD during quiet standing
bw <- mean(quiet$force_total)
bw_sd <- sd(quiet$force_total)

# 2. Onset threshold
threshold <- bw - 5 * bw_sd

# 3. First time the force drops below the threshold
onset_time <- cmj3$time_s[which(cmj3$force_total < threshold)[1]]
onset_time
# 1. Body weight and its SD during quiet standing
bw <- mean(quiet$force_total)
bw_sd <- sd(quiet$force_total)

# 2. Onset threshold
threshold <- bw - 5 * bw_sd

# 3. First time the force drops below the threshold
onset_time <- cmj3$time_s[which(cmj3$force_total < threshold)[1]]
onset_time








The coefficient of variation (CV)
The SD is in the units of the data, so you can’t compare the variability of, say, jump height (cm) and sprint time (s) directly. The coefficient of variation expresses the SD as a percentage of the mean:
\[CV = \frac{SD}{\bar{x}} \times 100\%\]
In sport science the CV is widely used to describe the consistency of repeated trials (test–retest reliability). A CV below about 5 % is generally considered good for jump height.

Athlete K’s three jump heights are given. Calculate their CV in % and store it in cv_height.










sd(height_cm) / mean(height_cm) * 100




height_cm <- c(40.4, 39.6, 41.3)

# CV in %
cv_height <- sd(height_cm) / mean(height_cm) * 100
cv_height
height_cm <- c(40.4, 39.6, 41.3)

# CV in %
cv_height <- sd(height_cm) / mean(height_cm) * 100
cv_height







What are the units of the variance of jump heights measured in cm?

cm
cm²
%


The variance averages squared deviations, so its unit is cm². That’s why we usually report the SD (cm), its square root.



If you add 10 cm to every jump height (e.g. a measurement offset), what happens to the SD?

It increases by 10 cm
It stays the same
It increases by 10 %


Every value and the mean move by 10 cm, so the deviations from the mean don’t change, and neither does the SD. Spread is about distances between values, not their location.

title: 2.3 Measures of spread
text:
Quartiles, quantiles and quintiles
The SD works best for roughly symmetric data. A second family of spread measures is based on sorting the data, just like the median.
Quantiles divide sorted data into equal-sized parts. The 0.9 quantile (also called the 90th percentile) is the value below which 90 % of the observations lie. Special names exist for some common divisions:



Name
Divides the data into
Cut points




Quartiles
4 parts
25 %, 50 %, 75 % (Q1, Q2 = median, Q3)


Quintiles
5 parts
20 %, 40 %, 60 %, 80 %


Deciles
10 parts
10 %, 20 %, …, 90 %


Percentiles
100 parts
1 %, 2 %, …, 99 %



The function quantile() gives the quartiles (plus min and max) by default:








So 25 % of participants scored 18 or less (Q1) and 75 % scored 25 or less (Q3). Use the probs argument for other quantiles:








seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1) creates the sequence 0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9.
The distance between Q3 and Q1 is the interquartile range (IQR): the range of the middle 50 % of the data. Like the median, it’s robust to extreme values.








Percentiles are used a lot for normative data: “Your Mini-BESTest score is at the 20th percentile for your age group”, or physical-fitness test norms for children.


Calculate the quintiles of balance$tmt_a_s (Trail Making Test A time) and store them in tmt_quintiles.
Calculate the IQR of balance$tmt_a_s and store it in tmt_iqr.











probs = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8) and IQR(balance$tmt_a_s).




# 1. Quintiles of TMT-A time
tmt_quintiles <- quantile(balance$tmt_a_s, probs = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8))

# 2. Interquartile range
tmt_iqr <- IQR(balance$tmt_a_s)

tmt_quintiles
tmt_iqr
# 1. Quintiles of TMT-A time
tmt_quintiles <- quantile(balance$tmt_a_s, probs = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8))

# 2. Interquartile range
tmt_iqr <- IQR(balance$tmt_a_s)

tmt_quintiles
tmt_iqr







Making quintile groups
Researchers often split participants into groups using quantiles, e.g. “the lowest 20 % of balance scores”. The function cut() does this when you give it the quantiles as breaks:








Each quintile group contains about 20 % of the participants (≈33 people), and you can see the median balance score drop in the oldest quintiles.

A player’s sprint time is at the 80th percentile of the team’s 30 m times. What does that mean?

They are faster than 80 % of the team
80 % of the team’s times are equal to or lower than theirs, so they are among the slower players
Their time is 80 % of the team’s best time


Percentiles describe the position in the sorted data. For sprint times, a lower value is better, so a time at the 80th percentile is slower than 80 % of the team. Always check whether higher or lower is better!

title: 2.3 Measures of spread
text:
Finding outliers using the IQR
An outlier is an observation that lies unusually far from the rest. A widely used rule (by John Tukey, and the same one box plots use) flags values that lie more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles:
\[\text{lower fence} = Q_1 - 1.5 \times IQR \qquad \text{upper fence} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR\]
Values below the lower fence or above the upper fence are potential outliers. In a box plot, they are the dots beyond the whiskers.








The dots on the right are the participants the IQR rule flags in the Trail Making Test A.

Find the outliers in the Trail Making Test A times (tmt_a_s).

Calculate q1 and q3 with quantile() (probs 0.25 and 0.75) and iqr with IQR().
Calculate the upper_fence.
Create slow: the participants (rows of balance) whose tmt_a_s is above the upper fence. Then count them.












probs = 0.25, probs = 0.75, IQR(balance$tmt_a_s)
q3 + 1.5 * iqr
subset(balance, tmt_a_s > upper_fence)





# 1. Quartiles and IQR
q1 <- quantile(balance$tmt_a_s, probs = 0.25)
q3 <- quantile(balance$tmt_a_s, probs = 0.75)
iqr <- IQR(balance$tmt_a_s)

# 2. Upper fence
upper_fence <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr

# 3. Participants above the upper fence
slow <- subset(balance, tmt_a_s > upper_fence)
nrow(slow)
# 1. Quartiles and IQR
q1 <- quantile(balance$tmt_a_s, probs = 0.25)
q3 <- quantile(balance$tmt_a_s, probs = 0.75)
iqr <- IQR(balance$tmt_a_s)

# 2. Upper fence
upper_fence <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr

# 3. Participants above the upper fence
slow <- subset(balance, tmt_a_s > upper_fence)
nrow(slow)







An outlier is not automatically an error
What should you do with outliers? Never delete them automatically. First ask why a value is unusual:

Measurement or data-entry error (a jump height of 410 cm instead of 41.0 cm): correct it or remove it, and report that you did.
A genuine but extreme observation (a very slow participant, an elite athlete in a recreational group): keep it, and consider robust statistics (median, IQR).
Part of the phenomenon you’re studying: definitely keep it!

The force data shows the last case beautifully. Apply the IQR rule to all force samples of CMJ 3:
















Almost 300 samples are flagged, and they are exactly the propulsion and landing phases: the most important parts of the jump! Most of the recording is quiet standing, so the IQR rule considers everything else “unusual”. The lesson: outlier rules are tools for spotting values worth a second look, not for deciding what to delete. Always combine them with your knowledge of the data.

For a variable, Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 30. Above which value would an observation be flagged as an outlier?

35
45
60


IQR = 30 − 20 = 10. Upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 30 + 15 = 45.



You find a participant with a body mass of 7.2 kg in a dataset of adult runners. What should you do?

Keep it: outliers are real data
Delete the participant without mentioning it
Check the original records: it’s probably a data-entry error (72 kg), so correct it if you can, and document what you did


A 7.2 kg adult is impossible, so this is an error, not a genuine extreme value. Fix it from the source data if possible (otherwise set it to NA), and always report data cleaning decisions.



Which pair of statistics is most appropriate to describe a strongly skewed variable?

Mean and SD
Median and IQR
Mode and range


Both the median and the IQR are based on sorted positions, so extreme values in the tail affect them little. Mean and SD are best for roughly symmetric data.
