title: 2.1 What is statistics?
section: Meet the new dataset: countermovement jumps
text:
Meet the new dataset: countermovement jumps
The countermovement jump (CMJ) is one of the most common tests in sport science. The athlete stands still, dips down quickly and jumps as high as possible. In this module you’ll work with real data from Athlete K, a professional basketball player who performed three CMJs on a dual force platform: one plate under each foot.
A force platform measures the ground reaction force (GRF), in newtons (N), 500 times per second (500 Hz). The data frame cmj has been loaded for you:















Column
Meaning




trial
CMJ 1, CMJ 2 or CMJ 3


time_s
Time since the start of the recording (s); a new value every 0.002 s


force_left, force_right
Vertical force under the left and right foot (N)


force_total
Left + right (N)



Let’s plot one jump. You know how to make a line plot from lesson 1.5:








Reading the curve from left to right:

Quiet standing (0–1.5 s): the force equals the athlete’s body weight (about 726 N).
Unweighting: the athlete starts to dip, and the force drops below body weight.
Braking and propulsion (≈2.0–2.6 s): the athlete stops the dip and pushes off, with force rising to about 2.5 × body weight.
Flight: no contact, so the force is 0 N.
Landing (≈3.2 s): a large impact peak, then the athlete settles back to body weight.

Each jump produces thousands of numbers. Statistics helps us turn them into a few meaningful ones.

title: 2.1 What is statistics?
text:
What is statistics?
Statistics is the science of collecting, organising, summarising and interpreting data in order to answer questions and make decisions under uncertainty.
Why is there uncertainty? Because of variability. Measure the same thing twice and you get two different answers. Here are Athlete K’s three jumps, performed one minute apart:








The jump heights are 40.4, 39.6 and 41.3 cm. So what is Athlete K’s “real” jump height? If he jumps 42 cm next month, has he improved, or is that just normal variation? Questions like these are what statistics is for. Other examples from sport and exercise science:

Does a 6-week plyometric programme improve jump height more than regular training?
Is the left leg producing more force than the right (asymmetry)?
Do older adults with a history of falls have worse balance?
What is a “normal” Mini-BESTest score for a 70-year-old?


Athlete K’s three jump heights differ (40.4, 39.6 and 41.3 cm). What is the best explanation?

The force platform is broken
Variability: no person performs exactly the same movement twice, and measurements contain small errors
One of the jumps must be a mistake and should be deleted


Variability is normal and everywhere: biological variation (fatigue, technique, motivation) plus measurement error. Statistics gives us tools to describe it and to decide whether a difference is bigger than this normal variation.

title: 2.1 What is statistics?
text:
Descriptive and inferential statistics
Statistics has two main branches.
Descriptive statistics summarise the data you actually have: averages, ranges, tables and plots. “Athlete K’s mean jump height over these three trials was 40.4 cm.” “The 163 participants in the balance study were aged 18 to 86 years.” No conclusions beyond the data are drawn.
Inferential statistics use a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, and say how certain those conclusions are. “Older adults score lower on the Mini-BESTest than younger adults (p < 0.001).” This is a claim about all older and younger adults, based on only 163 of them.
Two pairs of terms go with this distinction:








Term
Meaning
Example




Population
Everyone (or everything) you want to draw conclusions about
All community-dwelling adults; every jump Athlete K could ever make


Sample
The part of the population you actually measured
The 163 participants in the balance study; Athlete K’s 3 jumps


Parameter
A number describing the population (usually unknown)
The true mean Mini-BESTest score of all older adults


Statistic
A number calculated from the sample, used to estimate the parameter
The mean Mini-BESTest score of the 76 older participants



This module focuses on descriptive statistics, plus two key ideas (the normal distribution and the central limit theorem) that form the bridge to inferential statistics in Module 4.

Calculate a descriptive statistic: Athlete K’s mean jump height across the three trials. Use the height_cm column of jumps.










Select the column with $ and use mean(): mean(jumps$height_cm).




# Mean jump height of Athlete K
mean(jumps$height_cm)
# Mean jump height of Athlete K
mean(jumps$height_cm)







“Based on our sample of 40 players, U18 basketball players in Greece jump on average 38 cm (95 % CI 36–40 cm).” Which type of statistics is this?

Descriptive
Inferential


The statement draws a conclusion about all U18 players in Greece (the population) from 40 players (a sample), and expresses the uncertainty with a confidence interval. That’s inference.



“In our study, 42 of the 163 participants reported at least one fall in the past year.” Which type of statistics is this?

Descriptive
Inferential


It simply reports what happened in the sample, with no generalisation to a population.



A researcher measures the VO₂max of 25 university rowers to learn about the fitness of university rowers in general. What are the population and the sample?

Population = the 25 rowers; sample = all university rowers
Population = all university rowers; sample = the 25 rowers measured
Both are the 25 rowers


The population is the whole group you want to know about; the sample is the subset you actually measured.

title: 2.1 What is statistics?
text:
Data type classification
Before you summarise or analyse a variable, you must know what type of data it is, because that determines which statistics and plots make sense. For example, a mean is meaningful for jump height but not for playing position.










Type
Sub-type
Description
Sport-science examples
Store in R as




Numerical (quantitative)
Continuous
Measured; any value in a range (decimals possible)
jump height, force, body mass, sprint time, VO₂max
numeric



Discrete
Counted; whole numbers only
number of falls, goals, repetitions, injuries per season
numeric / integer


Categorical (qualitative)
Nominal
Categories with no natural order
sex, sport, playing position, left/right leg
factor



Ordinal
Categories with a natural order
activity level (low < moderate < high), RPE category, injury severity
ordered factor









TipWatch out for numbers that are really categories



A participant ID (1, 2, 3, …) or a shirt number is stored as a number, but it’s really a nominal label: an “average shirt number” means nothing. Similarly, scale scores like the Mini-BESTest (0–28) or a Likert item (1–5) are technically ordinal, although sum scores like the Mini-BESTest are often treated as numerical in practice.


Let’s look at the balance dataset with this lens:















Column
Type




age, height_cm, mass_kg, bmi, tmt_a_s, tmt_b_s
continuous


falls_12m
discrete (a count)


sex, nationality, illness, age_group
nominal


activity, fear_falling
ordinal


subject
an ID label (nominal), not a quantity



Notice that R reads activity as chr (character). R doesn’t know it’s ordinal: you have to tell it, as you learned in lesson 1.3.


Convert balance$sex into a (nominal) factor and store it in sex_f.
Convert balance$activity into an ordered factor activity_f with the levels Low < Moderate < High.
On the last line, use table() to count the participants in each activity level.












factor(balance$sex)
ordered = TRUE, levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")
table(activity_f)





# 1. Nominal
sex_f <- factor(balance$sex)

# 2. Ordinal
activity_f <- factor(balance$activity, ordered = TRUE, levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

# 3. Count per activity level
table(activity_f)
# 1. Nominal
sex_f <- factor(balance$sex)

# 2. Ordinal
activity_f <- factor(balance$activity, ordered = TRUE, levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

# 3. Count per activity level
table(activity_f)






Now classify some variables yourself.

The peak force during a CMJ (in N) is…

continuous
discrete
ordinal


Force is measured on a continuous scale and can take any value, e.g. 1888.2 N.



The number of successful free throws out of 10 is…

continuous
discrete
nominal


It’s a count, so it can only be a whole number from 0 to 10.



Rating of perceived exertion recorded as very light / light / moderate / hard / very hard is…

nominal
ordinal
continuous


These are categories with a clear order, but the “distance” between them is not necessarily equal. That’s the hallmark of ordinal data.



The trial column of cmj (CMJ 1, CMJ 2, CMJ 3) is best treated as…

continuous, because it contains numbers
nominal: it’s a label identifying the trial
discrete, because you can count trials


“CMJ 1/2/3” is a label. You might argue for ordinal (trials happened in order), but you wouldn’t calculate an average trial. It identifies groups of measurements.

title: 2.1 What is statistics?
text:
Lesson summary

Statistics turns data into answers while accounting for variability.
Descriptive statistics summarise the data you have; inferential statistics generalise from a sample to a population.
Numerical data is continuous (measured) or discrete (counted); categorical data is nominal (no order) or ordinal (ordered).
In R: numbers → numeric, nominal → factor(), ordinal → factor(..., ordered = TRUE, levels = ...).


Scratchpad
cmj, jumps and balance are loaded. Try plotting force_left and force_right of CMJ 1 to see the two legs separately.

title: 1.5 Plotting with ggplot2
text:
The grammar of graphics
ggplot2 is the most popular plotting package in R. It builds every plot from the same three ingredients:

data: a data frame,
aesthetics (aes()): which columns go on which visual property, e.g. x, y, colour, fill,
geoms (geom_...()): the geometric shapes that represent the data, e.g. points, bars, boxes, lines.

You start a plot with ggplot() and add layers with +:
ggplot(data = my_data, aes(x = column1, y = column2)) +
  geom_point()
Before you can use ggplot2 you load it with library(ggplot2). On this page that’s already done for you. Run the code below to see your first plot:














ImportantPut the + at the end of the line



The + must be at the end of a line, not at the start of the next one. Otherwise R thinks the plot is finished and doesn’t know what to do with the next line.

title: 1.5 Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Histograms
A histogram shows the distribution of one numeric variable: the x-axis is divided into intervals (bins) and the height of each bar is the number of observations in that bin. Only an x aesthetic is needed.








The binwidth argument sets the width of each bin (here 2 points). Always try a few values: too wide hides details, too narrow makes the histogram noisy.

fill and colour
Two aesthetics control colour, and beginners often mix them up:

fill is the colour inside a shape (the bars),
colour (or color) is the colour of the outline (or of points and lines).










Make a histogram of participants’ age with a binwidth of 5 years, dark-green bars (fill = "darkgreen") and black outlines (colour = "black").










aes(x = age) and geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "darkgreen", colour = "black").




ggplot(balance, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "darkgreen", colour = "black")
ggplot(balance, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "darkgreen", colour = "black")








Mapping fill to a variable
So far we set fill to one fixed colour. You can also map fill to a column inside aes(). ggplot2 then gives each group its own colour and adds a legend automatically:








alpha (0–1) makes the bars transparent so both groups are visible, and position = "identity" draws them on top of each other instead of stacking them.






TipThe golden rule




Inside aes() → the colour depends on the data: aes(fill = age_group)
Outside aes() → one fixed value for everything: geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue")




You write geom_histogram(aes(fill = "blue")). What happens?

All bars are blue
The bars get a default colour (salmon-red) and a legend with the label “blue” appears
R gives an error


Inside aes(), ggplot2 treats "blue" as a data value (a group called “blue”), not as a colour, so it picks its own colour and adds a legend. To make the bars blue, put it outside: geom_histogram(fill = "blue").



Which aesthetic changes the colour of the outline of histogram bars?

fill
colour
alpha


colour (or color) controls outlines, points and lines. fill controls the inside of shapes. alpha controls transparency.

title: 1.5 Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Scatter plots
A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables, one point per observation. Use geom_point().








Each point is a participant. There is a clear pattern: older participants tend to have lower Mini-BESTest scores. Note: size and alpha are set outside aes(), so they apply to all points.
For points, colour is the most important aesthetic (points have no inside to fill). Mapping it to a categorical variable shows groups:








You can add a trend line with geom_smooth(). method = "lm" draws a straight (linear regression) line, and se = FALSE hides the confidence band:








Because colour = sex is in the main ggplot() call, both layers use it, so you get one line per sex.

Make a scatter plot of Trail Making Test A time (tmt_a_s, x-axis) against Mini-BESTest score (minibest, y-axis), with the points coloured by age_group.










aes(x = tmt_a_s, y = minibest, colour = age_group) and the geom for points is geom_point().




ggplot(balance, aes(x = tmt_a_s, y = minibest, colour = age_group)) +
  geom_point()
ggplot(balance, aes(x = tmt_a_s, y = minibest, colour = age_group)) +
  geom_point()

title: 1.5 Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Box plots
A box plot summarises a numeric variable for each group. Put the grouping (categorical) variable on x and the numeric variable on y:








How to read it:

the thick line in the box is the median,
the box covers the middle 50 % of the data (from the 25th to the 75th percentile, the interquartile range, IQR),
the whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR of the box,
dots beyond the whiskers are potential outliers.

Box plots look better with fill. Map it to the same variable as x to colour each box (show.legend = FALSE hides the then-redundant legend):








Map fill to a different variable to compare subgroups side by side:









Make a box plot of fear-of-falling score (fes_total, y-axis) for each physical-activity level (activity, x-axis), with the boxes filled by activity. Because activity is an ordered factor, the boxes appear in a logical order: Low, Moderate, High.










aes(x = activity, y = fes_total, fill = activity) + geom_boxplot().




ggplot(balance, aes(x = activity, y = fes_total, fill = activity)) +
  geom_boxplot()
ggplot(balance, aes(x = activity, y = fes_total, fill = activity)) +
  geom_boxplot()







In a box plot, what does the line inside the box represent?

The mean
The median
The mode


The line is the median (50th percentile). Box plots don’t show the mean by default.

title: 1.5 Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Raincloud plots
Box plots hide the shape of the distribution and how many observations there are. A raincloud plot combines three layers to show everything at once:

a half-violin (“cloud”): the shape of the distribution,
a narrow box plot: the median and quartiles,
the raw data points (“rain”).

ggplot2 doesn’t have a raincloud geom, but because plots are built from layers, you can stack the three yourself. The half-violin comes from the ggdist package (stat_halfeye()), which is loaded on this page.








What the arguments do:

adjust controls the smoothness of the cloud (smaller = more detail),
justification moves the cloud away from the box,
.width = 0 and point_colour = NA hide the interval and point that stat_halfeye() draws by default,
geom_jitter() is geom_point() with a small random horizontal shift,
coord_flip() swaps x and y, giving the typical horizontal “raincloud” look.

Now you can see that the old group’s scores are spread out widely, while most young participants score close to the maximum: something a box plot alone doesn’t show.

The raincloud plot below is missing its rain. Complete it so it shows BMI (bmi) for each sex, and add the raw-data layer with geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.4).










Use y = bmi, and replace the second blank with geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.4).




ggplot(balance, aes(x = sex, y = bmi, fill = sex)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.6, width = 0.6, justification = -0.25,
               .width = 0, point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.4) +
  coord_flip()
ggplot(balance, aes(x = sex, y = bmi, fill = sex)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.6, width = 0.6, justification = -0.25,
               .width = 0, point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, alpha = 0.4) +
  coord_flip()







What is the main advantage of a raincloud plot over a box plot?

It is faster to draw
It shows the distribution’s shape and the raw data, not just summary statistics
It shows the mean and standard deviation


Box plots summarise data with five numbers. Two very different distributions (e.g. one with two peaks) can produce the same box. Raincloud plots show the shape and every observation as well.

title: 1.5 Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Line plots
Line plots connect observations in order, usually over time. They’re ideal for repeated measurements: heart rate during a test, force during a jump, performance over a season.
To practise, here is a small simulated dataset, hr_test: three athletes completed an incremental treadmill test, and their heart rate (hr, bpm) was recorded every minute.









Why you need group
Let’s try a line plot with just x and y:








That’s a mess! ggplot2 doesn’t know that the data belongs to three different athletes, so it draws one line that zig-zags between them. The group aesthetic tells ggplot2 which observations belong together:








Now there’s one line per athlete, but we can’t tell who is who. Mapping colour to athlete fixes that. Mapping a categorical variable to colour also groups the data automatically. Adding geom_point() marks the actual measurements:









Make a line plot of hr_test with minute on the x-axis and hr on the y-axis. Use group = athlete and colour = athlete, and add both geom_line() and geom_point().










aes(x = minute, y = hr, group = athlete, colour = athlete), then geom_line() + geom_point().




ggplot(hr_test, aes(x = minute, y = hr, group = athlete, colour = athlete)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
ggplot(hr_test, aes(x = minute, y = hr, group = athlete, colour = athlete)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()








Lines for group means
Line plots are also used to show summary values across ordered categories. The data frame best_by_age (created for you) contains the mean Mini-BESTest score for each age band and sex:









Plot best_by_age with age_band on the x-axis, minibest on the y-axis and one coloured line per sex. Because age_band is categorical, you must set group = sex for the lines to be drawn. Add points too.










Both blanks are sex.




ggplot(best_by_age, aes(x = age_band, y = minibest, group = sex, colour = sex)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
ggplot(best_by_age, aes(x = age_band, y = minibest, group = sex, colour = sex)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()







Your line plot shows a single zig-zag line instead of one line per participant. What’s the most likely fix?

Add fill = participant to aes()
Add group = participant (or colour = participant) to aes()
Replace geom_line() with geom_point()


Lines connect observations within a group. Without a group (or a discrete colour), ggplot2 puts all observations in one group and connects them all.

title: 1.5 Plotting with ggplot2
text:
Finishing touches: labels and themes
Good figures have clear axis labels with units. Add them with labs(), and change the overall look with a theme_...() function:








Try other themes: theme_classic(), theme_bw(), theme_light(). Module 3 covers customising plots in much more detail.

Match the question to the best plot: “How is jump height related to body mass in my team?”

Histogram
Scatter plot
Line plot


Two numeric variables measured on the same athletes → scatter plot. A histogram shows one variable’s distribution; a line plot shows change over time or ordered categories.

title: 1.3 Factors
section: What’s a factor and why would you use it?
text:
What’s a factor and why would you use it?
Many variables in sport science are categorical: they put each observation into one of a limited number of groups.

sex: F, M
playing position: goalkeeper, defender, midfielder, forward
test condition: eyes open / closed, firm surface / foam
age group: young, old

In R, categorical variables are stored as factors. A factor looks like a character vector, but R knows that the values are categories (called levels). That matters because statistical tests and plots treat categories differently from free text: they count them, compare groups, colour them and put them in a sensible order.
You create a factor with the function factor():








Notice the extra line Levels: F M in the output: R has found the two categories.

Eight balance trials were performed under these vision conditions. Convert vision_vector into a factor called factor_vision and print it.










Use factor(vision_vector), then write factor_vision on the last line.




vision_vector <- c("Open", "Closed", "Open", "Open", "Closed", "Closed", "Open", "Closed")

# Convert vision_vector to a factor
factor_vision <- factor(vision_vector)

# Print out factor_vision
factor_vision
vision_vector <- c("Open", "Closed", "Open", "Open", "Closed", "Closed", "Open", "Closed")

# Convert vision_vector to a factor
factor_vision <- factor(vision_vector)

# Print out factor_vision
factor_vision







Which of these variables should be stored as a factor?

Countermovement jump height (cm)
Type of footwear (barefoot, running shoe, minimalist)
Heart rate (bpm)


Footwear type is categorical: each trial belongs to one of a few groups. Jump height and heart rate are continuous measurements and should be numeric.

title: 1.3 Factors
text:
Factor levels
Data files often use short codes, like "F" and "M". The function levels() shows the categories of a factor, and you can also use it to rename them, which is useful for tables and plots:














WarningOrder matters!



When renaming, the new names are matched to the existing levels in order. Always check the current order with levels() first: here it is "F" "M" (alphabetical), so "Female" must come first.


You can also choose the order of the levels yourself when you create the factor, with the levels argument:









The vector group_vector codes participants as "Y" (young) or "O" (old).

Convert it to a factor factor_group.
Rename the levels to "Old" and "Young" (check the order!).











levels(factor(group_vector)) is "O" "Y" (alphabetical), so the new names must be c("Old", "Young").




group_vector <- c("Y", "O", "O", "Y", "Y", "O")

# Convert group_vector to a factor
factor_group <- factor(group_vector)

# Rename the levels
levels(factor_group) <- c("Old", "Young")

factor_group
group_vector <- c("Y", "O", "O", "Y", "Y", "O")

# Convert group_vector to a factor
factor_group <- factor(group_vector)

# Rename the levels
levels(factor_group) <- c("Old", "Young")

factor_group

title: 1.3 Factors
text:
Summarizing a factor
How many observations fall into each category? summary() gives a different answer for a character vector and a factor:








Now let’s use real data. The trials dataset contains all 1,930 standing-balance trials from the balance study. It has been loaded for you. Each trial was done with eyes Open or Closed on a Firm surface or Foam. The $ sign picks out one column (more on that in the next lesson):








The function table() gives the same counts, and can also cross-tabulate two factors:









Convert the Surface column of trials into a factor called surface_factor and summarise it with summary() on the last line.










The column is trials$Surface. Then use summary(surface_factor).




# Convert the Surface column to a factor
surface_factor <- factor(trials$Surface)

# Summarise surface_factor
summary(surface_factor)
# Convert the Surface column to a factor
surface_factor <- factor(trials$Surface)

# Summarise surface_factor
summary(surface_factor)







In the output of table(trials$Vision, trials$Surface), how many trials were done with eyes closed on foam?

474
487
480


Find the row Closed and the column Foam: 474 trials. Run the code above again if you need to check.

title: 1.3 Factors
text:
Ordered factors
Sex, vision and surface are nominal variables: there is no natural order between the categories. Other categorical variables do have an order. These are called ordinal variables:

physical activity level: Low < Moderate < High
fear of falling: Low < Moderate < High
injury severity: minor < moderate < severe

For ordinal variables you create an ordered factor by adding ordered = TRUE and listing the levels from lowest to highest:








The levels are now printed with < signs between them, showing the order.

The physical-activity levels of six participants are given in activity_vector. Create an ordered factor activity_factor with the order Low < Moderate < High.










Use ordered = TRUE and levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High").




activity_vector <- c("High", "Low", "Moderate", "Moderate", "High", "Low")

# Create an ordered factor
activity_factor <- factor(activity_vector,
                          ordered = TRUE,
                          levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

activity_factor
activity_vector <- c("High", "Low", "Moderate", "Moderate", "High", "Low")

# Create an ordered factor
activity_factor <- factor(activity_vector,
                          ordered = TRUE,
                          levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

activity_factor

title: 1.3 Factors
text:
Ordered factors (example)
Let’s apply this to the real data. The balance dataset (one row per participant) has a column activity with each participant’s activity level. By default R would order the levels alphabetically (High, Low, Moderate), which makes no sense in a table or plot:









Create an ordered factor fear_factor from the column balance$fear_falling (fear of falling), with the levels Low < Moderate < High. Then summarise it.










The first argument is balance$fear_falling. The levels are c("Low", "Moderate", "High").




# Ordered factor of fear of falling
fear_factor <- factor(balance$fear_falling,
                      ordered = TRUE,
                      levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

# Summarise fear_factor
summary(fear_factor)
# Ordered factor of fear of falling
fear_factor <- factor(balance$fear_falling,
                      ordered = TRUE,
                      levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

# Summarise fear_factor
summary(fear_factor)

title: 1.3 Factors
text:
Comparing ordered factors
Because an ordered factor knows the order of its levels, you can compare its elements with <, >, == and so on. This doesn’t work for unordered factors (try it and R will give a warning).










Store the activity level of the first participant in participant1 and that of the third participant in participant3.
On the last line, check whether participant 1 is more active than participant 3.











Select with square brackets: activity_factor[1] and activity_factor[3]. Then compare with participant1 > participant3.




activity_factor <- factor(c("High", "Low", "Moderate", "Moderate", "High", "Low"),
                          ordered = TRUE, levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

# Select participants 1 and 3
participant1 <- activity_factor[1]
participant3 <- activity_factor[3]

# Is participant 1 more active than participant 3?
participant1 > participant3
activity_factor <- factor(c("High", "Low", "Moderate", "Moderate", "High", "Low"),
                          ordered = TRUE, levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

# Select participants 1 and 3
participant1 <- activity_factor[1]
participant3 <- activity_factor[3]

# Is participant 1 more active than participant 3?
participant1 > participant3







You compare two elements of an unordered factor, e.g. factor_sex[1] > factor_sex[2]. What happens?

R compares them alphabetically
R returns NA with a warning that > is not meaningful for factors
R returns TRUE


For nominal factors there is no order, so “greater than” has no meaning. R warns you and returns NA. Use ordered = TRUE when the categories have a natural order.



You create factor(c("Low", "High", "Moderate")) without setting the levels. In what order are the levels?

Low, Moderate, High
In the order they appear: Low, High, Moderate
Alphabetical: High, Low, Moderate


By default, R sorts the levels alphabetically. That’s why you should specify levels = ... for ordinal variables.

title: 1.3 Factors
text:
Lesson summary

Categorical variables are stored as factors: factor(x).
levels() shows (and renames) the categories; set your own order with factor(x, levels = ...).
summary() and table() count observations per category; table(a, b) cross-tabulates.
Ordinal variables become ordered factors with ordered = TRUE, and their elements can be compared with < and >.


Scratchpad
The balance and trials datasets are loaded here too.

title: 1.1 R basics
text:
Why R?
Sport and exercise scientists collect a lot of data: jump heights from force plates, heart rates from chest straps, GPS distances, questionnaire scores, lab test results. Spreadsheets are fine for small tasks, but they become slow and error-prone as data grows. R is a free programming language designed for data analysis and statistics. With R you write down every step of your analysis as code, so it is reproducible: you (or your supervisor) can re-run it at any time and get exactly the same result.

title: 1.1 R basics
text:
Arithmetic with R
In its most basic form, R is a powerful calculator. These are the arithmetic operators:



Operator
Meaning
Example
Result




+
addition
5 + 3
8


-
subtraction
5 - 3
2


*
multiplication
5 * 3
15


/
division
6 / 4
1.5


^
exponentiation (power)
2 ^ 3
8


%%
modulo (remainder of a division)
7 %% 3
1



R follows the usual order of operations: brackets first, then powers, then multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction. Run the code below, then change it and run it again. This box is your console for experimenting.








Each line produces its own output, shown below the code. Lines starting with # are comments: R ignores them, and you use them to explain your code to humans.

An athlete completes 3 laps of 400 m followed by 4 laps of 200 m. Write a single line of R code that calculates the total distance in metres.










Multiply the number of laps by the lap length for each part, then add the two parts: 3 * ___ + 4 * ___.




# Total distance in metres
3 * 400 + 4 * 200
# Total distance in metres
3 * 400 + 4 * 200







A 1RM (one-repetition maximum) test gives 140 kg. Your athlete should train at 75 % of their 1RM. Calculate the training load in kg.










75 % is the same as 0.75. Multiply it by 140.




# 75 % of a 140 kg 1RM
140 * 0.75
# 75 % of a 140 kg 1RM
140 * 0.75







What does R return for 2 + 3 * 2?

10
8
7


Multiplication is done before addition: 3 * 2 = 6, and then 2 + 6 = 8. If you wanted 10 you would need brackets: (2 + 3) * 2.



What is the result of 17 %% 5?

3.4
3
2


%% gives the remainder of a division. 5 goes into 17 three times (15), with 2 left over.

title: 1.1 R basics
text:
Variable assignment
A basic concept in programming is the variable. A variable lets you store a value (e.g. 52) or an object (e.g. a whole dataset) under a name, so you can use it later.
In R you assign a value to a variable with the assignment operator <- (a “less than” sign followed by a minus). Read it as “gets”:
vo2max <- 52     # "vo2max gets 52"
After that, typing the variable’s name prints its value:














TipNaming rules



Variable names can contain letters, numbers, _ and ., but must start with a letter. They are case sensitive: vo2max and VO2max are two different variables. Choose names that describe the content, like jump_height or resting_hr.



Create a variable called resting_hr and assign the value 58 (beats per minute) to it. Then print it by typing its name on a new line.










Use resting_hr <- 58 on the first line, and just resting_hr on the next line.




# Assign the value 58 to resting_hr
resting_hr <- 58

# Print out the value of resting_hr
resting_hr
# Assign the value 58 to resting_hr
resting_hr <- 58

# Print out the value of resting_hr
resting_hr

title: 1.1 R basics
text:
Variable assignment (2)
Variables become really useful when you combine them. Suppose an athlete’s best lifts are stored in variables. You can calculate with the names instead of the numbers:








If the athlete improves, you only change the value once and every calculation that uses the variable updates automatically.

A powerlifting total is the sum of the best squat, bench press and deadlift.

Assign 150 to squat_kg, 95 to bench_kg and 180 to deadlift_kg.
Create a variable total_kg that is the sum of the three lifts (use the variable names, not the numbers).
Print total_kg.











The total is squat_kg + bench_kg + deadlift_kg. Print it by writing total_kg on the last line.




# Assign the three lifts
squat_kg <- 150
bench_kg <- 95
deadlift_kg <- 180

# Create total_kg using the three variables
total_kg <- squat_kg + bench_kg + deadlift_kg

# Print total_kg
total_kg
# Assign the three lifts
squat_kg <- 150
bench_kg <- 95
deadlift_kg <- 180

# Create total_kg using the three variables
total_kg <- squat_kg + bench_kg + deadlift_kg

# Print total_kg
total_kg

title: 1.1 R basics
text:
Variable assignment (3)
What happens if you try to add a number and a piece of text? Run this code and read the error message:








R complains: “non-numeric argument to binary operator”. The quotation marks around "0.15" make it text, not a number, and you can’t do arithmetic with text. Error messages may look scary, but they are R’s way of telling you exactly what went wrong. Reading them carefully is an important skill.

Fix the code so that total_time is calculated correctly. Don’t change the numbers, only the way one of them is written.










Remove the quotation marks around 0.15 so that R treats it as a number.




sprint_time <- 11.2
reaction_time <- 0.15

total_time <- sprint_time + reaction_time
total_time
sprint_time <- 11.2
reaction_time <- 0.15

total_time <- sprint_time + reaction_time
total_time







After running jump <- 35 and then jump <- jump + 5, what is the value of jump?

35
40
An error, because jump already exists


The right-hand side is calculated first using the old value (35 + 5 = 40), and the result is then stored in jump, overwriting the old value. Overwriting variables is allowed in R.

title: 1.1 R basics
text:
Basic data types in R
R works with several data types. The four you will meet most often are:








Type
What it stores
Examples




numeric
Decimal numbers
4.5, 72, -0.3


integer
Whole numbers (written with an L)
4L, 12L


character
Text (also called strings), always in quotes
"Maria", "midfielder"


logical
TRUE or FALSE (no quotes!)
TRUE, FALSE



Note that numbers like 72 are numeric by default; R only makes them integers if you add an L. In practice, you rarely need to worry about that difference.









Create the following variables describing a basketball player:

player with the text Nikos,
height_m with the number 1.98,
starter with the logical value TRUE.











Text needs quotation marks ("Nikos"), numbers don’t (1.98), and logical values are written in capitals without quotes (TRUE).




# Character: the player's name
player <- "Nikos"

# Numeric: height in metres
height_m <- 1.98

# Logical: is he in the starting five?
starter <- TRUE
# Character: the player's name
player <- "Nikos"

# Numeric: height in metres
height_m <- 1.98

# Logical: is he in the starting five?
starter <- TRUE

title: 1.1 R basics
text:
What’s that data type?
When R gives you an unexpected error, the reason is often that a value has a different type than you thought (like "0.15" earlier). You can ask R for the type of any value or variable with the function class():









Three variables are created for you. Use class() to find the data type of sport (as the last line of your code).










Put the name of the variable inside the brackets: class(sport).




sport <- "rowing"
distance_m <- 2000
personal_best <- FALSE

# Check the class of sport
class(sport)
sport <- "rowing"
distance_m <- 2000
personal_best <- FALSE

# Check the class of sport
class(sport)







What does class("72") return?

"numeric"
"integer"
"character"
"logical"


Anything inside quotation marks is text, so "72" is a character value even though it looks like a number.



Which of these values is a logical?

"FALSE"
FALSE
false


Logical values are written in capitals without quotes: TRUE and FALSE. "FALSE" is text, and false (lower case) is not recognised by R. It would look for a variable called false.

The datasets

Balance dataset (balance)
A real, open dataset from a study of standing balance in 163 adults aged 18 to 86 (Santos & Duarte, 2016, PeerJ, 4:e2648). Each row is one participant. The variables you will use most:







Column
Meaning




subject
Participant ID


age, age_group
Age in years; Young (< 60) or Old (≥ 60)


sex
F or M


height_cm, mass_kg, bmi, foot_cm
Anthropometry


falls_12m
Number of falls in the past 12 months


fes_total, fear_falling
Short Falls Efficacy Scale (7–28, higher = more concern) and its category (Low, Moderate, High)


activity
Physical-activity level from the IPAQ questionnaire (Low, Moderate, High)


tmt_a_s, tmt_b_s
Trail Making Test parts A and B, in seconds (cognitive function)


minibest
Mini-BESTest total score, 0–28 (higher = better dynamic balance)



Here is a peek. Press Run Code:










Balance trials (trials)
Every participant performed several 60-second standing trials with eyes open or closed, on a firm surface or foam. The trials data has one row per trial (1,930 trials) with the columns Trial, Subject, Vision, Surface, AgeGroup and Gender. You’ll use it when learning about factors.


Countermovement jumps (cmj)
Raw ground-reaction-force data from three countermovement jumps by a professional basketball player (anonymised as Athlete K), recorded on a dual force platform (one plate per foot) at 500 Hz. Used in Module 2.







Column
Meaning




trial
CMJ 1, CMJ 2 or CMJ 3


time_s
Time (s), one sample every 0.002 s


force_left, force_right
Vertical force under the left and right foot (N)


force_total
Left + right (N)





Jump-testing squad (squad)
CMJ force-platform variables of 84 professional athletes (42 basketball, 42 soccer players), one row per athlete, with names replaced by codes (B01–B42, S01–S42). It includes body mass and height, jump height, phase durations, mean and peak force, impulse, power and velocity (mostly per kg body mass), countermovement depth, eccentric RFD, RSImod and vertical stiffness. A full description is in lesson 3.1. Used in Modules 3 and 4.


Repeated jumps (trials)
Three consecutive CMJs of 56 professional basketball and soccer players (codes A01–A56): athlete, sport, trial (1–3), the body mass estimated by the force platform in that trial (body_mass_kg), and jump_height_cm. Used for reliability analysis in lesson 4.9.

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
The story for this lesson
You are coaching a triathlete. Every weekday they run and cycle, and you record the distances (in km). By the end of the lesson you’ll be able to answer questions such as “How much did they train in total?”, “On which days did they run more than 10 km?” and “What was their average cycling distance early in the week?”

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Create a vector
A vector is a sequence of values of the same type. You create one with the combine function c(), separating the values with commas:








Most data you collect is naturally a vector: the jump heights of a team, the heart rate every second, the names of all participants.

The triathlete’s distances from Monday to Friday are:

running: 8, 12, 5, 15, 10 km
cycling: 20, 0, 35, 15, 25 km

Create the vector running_km (given) and the vector cycling_km in the same order.










Use the same pattern as running_km: c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25).




# Running distances, Monday to Friday
running_km <- c(8, 12, 5, 15, 10)

# Cycling distances, Monday to Friday
cycling_km <- c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25)
# Running distances, Monday to Friday
running_km <- c(8, 12, 5, 15, 10)

# Cycling distances, Monday to Friday
cycling_km <- c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25)







What happens if you combine different types, e.g. c(12, "rest", 8)?

R gives an error
Everything is converted to text (character)
R drops "rest" and keeps the numbers


A vector can only hold one type. R converts all values to the most flexible type, here character: "12" "rest" "8". Try class(c(12, "rest", 8)) in a code box!

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Naming a vector
Looking at running_km, it isn’t obvious which value belongs to which day. You can give each element a name with the names() function:








If you need the same names for several vectors, store them in a vector first and reuse it. That saves typing and avoids typos:
days_vector <- c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday")
names(running_km) <- days_vector

The vector days_vector is created for you. Use it to name both running_km and cycling_km.










Put days_vector on the right-hand side of both assignments.




running_km <- c(8, 12, 5, 15, 10)
cycling_km <- c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25)
days_vector <- c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday")

# Assign the names of the days to running_km and cycling_km
names(running_km) <- days_vector
names(cycling_km) <- days_vector
running_km <- c(8, 12, 5, 15, 10)
cycling_km <- c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25)
days_vector <- c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday")

# Assign the names of the days to running_km and cycling_km
names(running_km) <- days_vector
names(cycling_km) <- days_vector

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Calculating total training volume (example 1)
Arithmetic on vectors works element by element. If you add two vectors of the same length, R adds the first elements together, then the second elements, and so on:








This is extremely handy: with one line you can calculate a value for every day, every athlete or every trial.

Calculate the total distance per day (running + cycling) and store it in total_daily. Then print it.










Add the two vectors: running_km + cycling_km.




days_vector <- c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday")
running_km <- c(8, 12, 5, 15, 10)
cycling_km <- c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25)
names(running_km) <- days_vector
names(cycling_km) <- days_vector

# Total distance per day
total_daily <- running_km + cycling_km

# Print total_daily
total_daily
days_vector <- c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday")
running_km <- c(8, 12, 5, 15, 10)
cycling_km <- c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25)
names(running_km) <- days_vector
names(cycling_km) <- days_vector

# Total distance per day
total_daily <- running_km + cycling_km

# Print total_daily
total_daily

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Calculating total training volume (example 2)
Now let’s summarise the whole week. The function sum() adds up all elements of a vector, and mean() gives the average:








You can also compare values with >, < and ==. The result is a logical value:










Calculate the weekly running total and store it in total_running.
Calculate the weekly cycling total and store it in total_cycling.
On the last line, check whether the triathlete cycled more than they ran (total_cycling > total_running).











Use sum(running_km) and sum(cycling_km), then compare them with >.




running_km <- c(8, 12, 5, 15, 10)
cycling_km <- c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25)

# Weekly totals
total_running <- sum(running_km)
total_cycling <- sum(cycling_km)

# Did they cycle more than they ran?
total_cycling > total_running
running_km <- c(8, 12, 5, 15, 10)
cycling_km <- c(20, 0, 35, 15, 25)

# Weekly totals
total_running <- sum(running_km)
total_cycling <- sum(cycling_km)

# Did they cycle more than they ran?
total_cycling > total_running







What does c(2, 4, 6) * 2 return?

24
4 8 12
2 4 6 2


Arithmetic is applied to each element: 2×2, 4×2 and 6×2. This is called vectorisation, and it’s one of R’s superpowers.

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Vector selection (indexing)
Often you only need part of a vector. You select elements with square brackets [ ]. Inside the brackets you put the position(s) you want. In R, the first element has position 1.














Tip



The shorthand c(Monday = 8, Tuesday = 12, ...) creates a vector and names it in one step.




Select the cycling distance on Wednesday and store it in cycling_wednesday.
Select the cycling distances from Tuesday to Thursday (use :) and store them in cycling_midweek.
Select Monday and Friday by name and store them in cycling_edges.











Wednesday is the 3rd element. Tuesday to Thursday is 2:4. For names, use c("Monday", "Friday").




cycling_km <- c(Monday = 20, Tuesday = 0, Wednesday = 35, Thursday = 15, Friday = 25)

# Wednesday (by position)
cycling_wednesday <- cycling_km[3]

# Tuesday to Thursday (use :)
cycling_midweek <- cycling_km[2:4]

# Monday and Friday (by name)
cycling_edges <- cycling_km[c("Monday", "Friday")]
cycling_km <- c(Monday = 20, Tuesday = 0, Wednesday = 35, Thursday = 15, Friday = 25)

# Wednesday (by position)
cycling_wednesday <- cycling_km[3]

# Tuesday to Thursday (use :)
cycling_midweek <- cycling_km[2:4]

# Monday and Friday (by name)
cycling_edges <- cycling_km[c("Monday", "Friday")]







hr <- c(62, 65, 61, 70). What does hr[-2] return?

65
62 61 70
61


A negative index removes that position, so you get everything except the second element.

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Selection by comparison: step 1
Comparison operators let you ask questions about every element of a vector at once:



Operator
Meaning




< / >
less than / greater than


<= / >=
less than or equal / greater than or equal


==
equal to (two = signs!)


!=
not equal to











The result is a logical vector: TRUE for the days with more than 9 km of running, FALSE for the others.

Create a logical vector long_ride that is TRUE for every day on which the triathlete cycled 20 km or more. Print it.










“20 km or more” means greater than or equal to: cycling_km >= 20.




cycling_km <- c(Monday = 20, Tuesday = 0, Wednesday = 35, Thursday = 15, Friday = 25)

# Which days had 20 km or more of cycling?
long_ride <- cycling_km >= 20

# Print long_ride
long_ride
cycling_km <- c(Monday = 20, Tuesday = 0, Wednesday = 35, Thursday = 15, Friday = 25)

# Which days had 20 km or more of cycling?
long_ride <- cycling_km >= 20

# Print long_ride
long_ride

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Selection by comparison: step 2
Here is the trick: you can put a logical vector inside the square brackets. R then keeps only the elements where the logical vector is TRUE:








You can also do it in one step: running_km[running_km > 9].

Use long_ride to select only the cycling distances of the long-ride days. Store the result in long_ride_km.










Put the logical vector inside the square brackets: cycling_km[long_ride].




cycling_km <- c(Monday = 20, Tuesday = 0, Wednesday = 35, Thursday = 15, Friday = 25)
long_ride <- cycling_km >= 20

# Select the distances of the long-ride days
long_ride_km <- cycling_km[long_ride]

long_ride_km
cycling_km <- c(Monday = 20, Tuesday = 0, Wednesday = 35, Thursday = 15, Friday = 25)
long_ride <- cycling_km >= 20

# Select the distances of the long-ride days
long_ride_km <- cycling_km[long_ride]

long_ride_km

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Advanced selection
You can combine selection with functions like mean() and sum() to answer more specific questions.








You can also combine conditions: & means and (both must be true), | means or (at least one must be true):










Calculate the average cycling distance from Monday to Wednesday, selecting the days by name. Store it in early_week_avg.
Count on how many days the triathlete did no cycling at all (== 0). Store it in rest_days.











Select with c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday"). For the rest days, cycling_km == 0 gives a logical vector, and sum() counts the TRUEs.




cycling_km <- c(Monday = 20, Tuesday = 0, Wednesday = 35, Thursday = 15, Friday = 25)

# Average cycling distance Monday to Wednesday
early_week_avg <- mean(cycling_km[c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday")])

# Number of days without cycling
rest_days <- sum(cycling_km == 0)

early_week_avg
rest_days
cycling_km <- c(Monday = 20, Tuesday = 0, Wednesday = 35, Thursday = 15, Friday = 25)

# Average cycling distance Monday to Wednesday
early_week_avg <- mean(cycling_km[c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday")])

# Number of days without cycling
rest_days <- sum(cycling_km == 0)

early_week_avg
rest_days







rpe <- c(6, 8, 3, 9, 7). What does rpe[rpe >= 7] return?

TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE
2 4 5
8 9 7


rpe >= 7 produces FALSE TRUE FALSE TRUE TRUE. Putting it in square brackets keeps the values where it is TRUE: 8, 9 and 7. (which(rpe >= 7) would give the positions 2, 4, 5.)



Which code counts how many values of rpe are above 5 and below 9?

sum(rpe > 5 | rpe < 9)
sum(rpe > 5 & rpe < 9)
rpe[rpe > 5 & rpe < 9]


Both conditions must hold, so you need & (and). sum() counts the TRUE values. The third option returns the values themselves (6 8 7), not how many there are.

title: 1.2 Vectors
text:
Lesson summary

Create vectors with c(). All elements must have the same type.
Name elements with names(x) <- ... or c(Monday = 8, ...).
Arithmetic is element-wise. sum() and mean() summarise a whole vector.
Select with [ ]: by position (x[3], x[2:4], x[-1]), by name (x["Monday"]) or with a logical vector (x[x > 9]).
Combine conditions with & (and) and | (or).


Scratchpad

title: 1.4 Data frames
text:
What’s a data frame?
So far you have stored one variable at a time in a vector. Real datasets contain many variables measured on the same participants: age, sex, body mass, test scores… These variables have different types (numeric, character, logical), so a single vector can’t hold them.
A data frame is R’s version of a spreadsheet table:

each row is one observation (e.g. one participant or one trial),
each column is one variable,
each column is a vector, so all values in a column have the same type, but different columns can have different types.

In this lesson you’ll work with the balance dataset: 163 adults aged 18–86 who completed a balance assessment (Santos & Duarte, 2016). It has been loaded for you with:
balance <- read.csv("data/balance.csv")
read.csv() reads a comma-separated file, the most common way to bring data into R. See How this course works for a description of all columns.

title: 1.4 Data frames
section: Quick, have a look at your dataset
text:
Quick, have a look at your dataset
Printing a whole dataset fills the screen. Usually you just want a quick look at the first or last rows. The function head() shows the first 6 rows and tail() the last 6:








You can ask for a different number of rows with a second argument: head(balance, n = 3). Other helpful functions are dim() (number of rows and columns), nrow(), ncol() and names() (the column names).

Show the last 4 rows of balance using tail().










tail() works just like head(): tail(balance, n = 4).




# Show the last 4 rows of balance
tail(balance, n = 4)
# Show the last 4 rows of balance
tail(balance, n = 4)







dim(balance) returns 163 18. What does this mean?

163 columns and 18 rows
163 rows (participants) and 18 columns (variables)
163 participants aged 18 or older


dim() always gives rows first, then columns. Each row is one participant, each column a variable.

title: 1.4 Data frames
section: Have a look at the structure
text:
Have a look at the structure
The function str() (structure) is the best first look at a new dataset. It shows:

the number of observations (rows) and variables (columns),
each column’s name and type (num, int, chr, logi),
the first few values of every column.









summary() goes one step further and gives descriptive statistics for every numeric column (minimum, quartiles, median, mean, maximum, and the number of missing values, NA):









Use summary() on the tmt_b_s column (Trail Making Test B time, in seconds) to find its median. Use the $ sign to select the column: balance$tmt_b_s.










Write summary(balance$tmt_b_s).




# Summarise the tmt_b_s column
summary(balance$tmt_b_s)
# Summarise the tmt_b_s column
summary(balance$tmt_b_s)







In the output of str(balance), the column sex is shown as chr. What does that tell you?

It contains numbers
It contains text (character values)
It is a factor


chr stands for character. Since R 4.0, read.csv() keeps text columns as character by default. Convert them with factor() when you need categories (for example for statistics or plots).

title: 1.4 Data frames
text:
Creating a data frame
You can also build a data frame yourself from vectors of equal length, with the function data.frame(). Each argument becomes a column: column_name = vector.

title: 1.4 Data frames
text:
Creating a data frame (example)

You tested five sprinters. Create a data frame called sprinters from the vectors below, with the columns in this order: athlete, sex, sprint_30m and injured. Then look at its structure with str().










data.frame(athlete, sex, sprint_30m, injured), then str(sprinters).




athlete    <- c("Eleni", "Marco", "Sofia", "Jonas", "Lea")
sex        <- c("F", "M", "F", "M", "F")
sprint_30m <- c(4.31, 3.98, 4.12, 4.05, 4.45)   # seconds
injured    <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)

# Create the data frame
sprinters <- data.frame(athlete, sex, sprint_30m, injured)

# Check its structure
str(sprinters)
athlete    <- c("Eleni", "Marco", "Sofia", "Jonas", "Lea")
sex        <- c("F", "M", "F", "M", "F")
sprint_30m <- c(4.31, 3.98, 4.12, 4.05, 4.45)   # seconds
injured    <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)

# Create the data frame
sprinters <- data.frame(athlete, sex, sprint_30m, injured)

# Check its structure
str(sprinters)

title: 1.4 Data frames
text:
Selection of data frame elements
Like vectors, you select from data frames with square brackets, but now you give two positions: [rows, columns].
my_df[1, 2]      # row 1, column 2
my_df[1:3, 2:4]  # rows 1-3, columns 2-4
my_df[1, ]       # all columns of row 1 (leave the column part empty)
my_df[, 2]       # all rows of column 2 (leave the row part empty)
Instead of column numbers you can use column names, which makes your code much easier to read:









Select the values of the columns age, sex and minibest for the first 10 participants (rows 1 to 10). Store the result in first10.










Rows: 1:10. Columns: c("age", "sex", "minibest"). Don’t forget the comma between them.




# Rows 1 to 10, columns age, sex and minibest
first10 <- balance[1:10, c("age", "sex", "minibest")]

first10
# Rows 1 to 10, columns age, sex and minibest
first10 <- balance[1:10, c("age", "sex", "minibest")]

first10

title: 1.4 Data frames
text:
Selection of data frame elements (2)
To select a whole column you’ll most often use the dollar sign: data$column. This returns the column as a vector, so everything from the vectors lesson works:








Now combine it with selection by comparison. A logical vector in the row position keeps only the rows where it is TRUE:








The function subset() does the same with less typing: you can use the column names directly.









Select all participants with a Mini-BESTest score below 15 (a sign of poor balance). Store them in poor_balance, using either subset() or square brackets. Then print only their age, sex, minibest and falls_12m.










subset(balance, minibest < 15) or balance[balance$minibest < 15, ].




# Participants with minibest below 15
poor_balance <- subset(balance, minibest < 15)

# Show age, sex, minibest and falls_12m
poor_balance[, c("age", "sex", "minibest", "falls_12m")]
# Participants with minibest below 15
poor_balance <- subset(balance, minibest < 15)

# Show age, sex, minibest and falls_12m
poor_balance[, c("age", "sex", "minibest", "falls_12m")]







What is the difference between balance$age and balance[1, ]?

balance$age is the whole age column; balance[1, ] is all variables of the first participant
Both return the age of the first participant
balance$age is the first row; balance[1, ] is the first column


$ selects a column by name (a vector of 163 ages). [1, ] selects row 1 with all columns (one participant).

title: 1.4 Data frames
text:
Exercise with datasets (1)

title: 2.2 Measures of center
text:
Measures of center
When you have many numbers, the first question is usually: what is a typical value? A measure of center (or central tendency) answers that with a single number. The three most common are:








Measure
Definition
In R




Mean
The sum of all values divided by how many there are (the “average”)
mean(x)


Median
The middle value once the data are sorted: half the values lie below it, half above
median(x)


Mode
The most frequent value
no built-in function; use table(x)



The mode is mainly useful for categorical data (“the most common playing position”). For numerical data, the mean and median are what you’ll use almost every time, so they’re the focus of this lesson.

title: 2.2 Measures of center
text:
Mean and median

The mean
The mean of n values \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\) is
\[\bar{x} = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n}{n} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]
You can calculate it step by step with sum() and length() (which counts the elements), or directly with mean():










The median
To find the median, sort the values and take the middle one:








With an even number of values there are two middle values, and the median is their average:









A coach records the number of repetitions to failure at 80 % 1RM for seven players. Calculate the mean by hand with sum() and length() and store it in mean_reps. Then calculate the median with median() and store it in median_reps.










sum(reps) / length(reps) and median(reps).




reps <- c(8, 10, 7, 9, 12, 8, 9)

# Mean by hand
mean_reps <- sum(reps) / length(reps)

# Median
median_reps <- median(reps)

mean_reps
median_reps
reps <- c(8, 10, 7, 9, 12, 8, 9)

# Mean by hand
mean_reps <- sum(reps) / length(reps)

# Median
median_reps <- median(reps)

mean_reps
median_reps








Real data: body weight from a force platform
Here is a classic sport-science use of the mean. Before a CMJ the athlete stands still, and the force platform measures their body weight. But the signal is never perfectly flat: the person sways slightly and the sensors have a little noise. The solution is to take the mean force during quiet standing.
The data frame cmj3 (third jump of Athlete K) is loaded. Let’s zoom in on the first 1.5 seconds:








The force wobbles by a few newtons around a central value. That central value is the body weight.


Create quiet: the rows of cmj3 where time_s is 1.5 s or less.
Calculate the athlete’s body weight in newtons as the mean of quiet$force_total. Store it in body_weight.
Convert body weight to body mass in kg by dividing by gravity, 9.81 m/s². Store it in body_mass.












subset(cmj3, time_s <= 1.5)
mean(quiet$force_total)
body_weight / 9.81





# 1. Quiet-standing phase
quiet <- subset(cmj3, time_s <= 1.5)

# 2. Body weight (N)
body_weight <- mean(quiet$force_total)

# 3. Body mass (kg)
body_mass <- body_weight / 9.81

body_weight
body_mass

Missing values
Real datasets have gaps. In R a missing value is written NA (not available). By default, mean() and median() return NA if any value is missing, which is R’s way of saying “I can’t be sure”. Add na.rm = TRUE (remove NAs) to ignore them:









What is the median of c(4, 1, 9, 6)?

6
5
5.5


Sorted: 1 4 6 9. With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values: (4 + 6) / 2 = 5. (The mean would be 20 / 4 = 5 too, but that’s a coincidence!)



What is the most appropriate “center” for playing position (guard, forward, center)?

The mean
The median
The mode


Playing position is nominal, so it has no numbers to average and no order to find a middle. The only measure that makes sense is the most frequent category, the mode.

title: 2.2 Measures of center
text:
Mean vs. median
For a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are almost the same. They differ when the data are skewed or contain extreme values, because:

the mean uses the actual size of every value, so a single extreme value pulls it towards itself,
the median only uses the order of the values, so it is robust: extreme values barely affect it.









One bad trial drops the mean by 5.6 cm, while the median changes by only 1 cm.

Skewed data
A distribution is right-skewed (positively skewed) when most values are low but a long tail stretches to the right, and left-skewed when the tail is on the left. In a skewed distribution the mean is pulled towards the tail:



Shape
Order




Symmetric
mean ≈ median


Right-skewed (tail to the right)
mean > median


Left-skewed (tail to the left)
mean < median



The Trail Making Test B time is strongly right-skewed: most participants finished within about 2 minutes, but some needed far longer (the test stops at 300 s). The histogram shows the mean (red) and median (blue):








geom_vline() draws a vertical line at the value given by xintercept.

Calculate the mean and median of balance$tmt_b_s and store them in tmt_mean and tmt_median. On the last line, calculate how many seconds the mean is larger than the median (tmt_mean - tmt_median).










mean(balance$tmt_b_s), median(balance$tmt_b_s), then tmt_mean - tmt_median.




tmt_mean <- mean(balance$tmt_b_s)
tmt_median <- median(balance$tmt_b_s)

# How much larger is the mean?
tmt_mean - tmt_median
tmt_mean <- mean(balance$tmt_b_s)
tmt_median <- median(balance$tmt_b_s)

# How much larger is the mean?
tmt_mean - tmt_median








A surprise in the force data
Now let’s compare the mean and median of the whole force recording of CMJ 3, from quiet standing through the jump and landing:








The mean force over the whole trial (≈727 N) equals body weight, even though the force went from 0 N (flight) up to more than 5700 N (landing)! This is no coincidence. The athlete starts and ends standing still, so (by Newton’s laws, the impulse–momentum relationship) the force above body weight and the force below body weight must exactly balance out over the trial. The mean “sees” the size of every value, so it finds that balance point.
The median just reports the middle value of all the samples (≈725 N). In other jumps, where the athlete spent more or less time at different force levels, the median can be far from body weight. Try median(subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 2")$force_total).

Use tapply() to calculate the median Mini-BESTest score for each age_group. tapply(values, groups, function) applies a function to the values of each group.










tapply(balance$minibest, balance$age_group, median). Note that the function name is given without brackets.




# Median minibest for each age group
tapply(balance$minibest, balance$age_group, median)
# Median minibest for each age group
tapply(balance$minibest, balance$age_group, median)







The annual salaries in a basketball team are: eleven players around €40,000 and one star player at €1,500,000. Which value best describes the typical salary?

The mean
The median
Both are equally good


The star’s salary is an extreme value that drags the mean up to about €160,000, a salary nobody on the team actually earns. The median (≈€40,000) represents the typical player.



A histogram of reaction times has a long tail to the right. Which statement is most likely true?

mean > median
mean < median
mean = median


In a right-skewed distribution, the few large values pull the mean towards the tail, above the median.



When should you prefer the mean over the median?

When the data contain extreme outliers
When the distribution is roughly symmetric without extreme values, because the mean then uses all the information in the data
Never: the median is always better


For symmetric data, the mean and median are similar, but the mean has useful mathematical properties (it’s the basis for SD, t-tests, ANOVA…). Use the median for skewed data or data with outliers, or report both.

title: 2.4 The normal distribution and the central limit theorem
text:
The normal distribution
Many measurements in biology and sport, such as body height, the small fluctuations of a force signal, or repeated measurements of the same athlete, follow a typical pattern: most values are close to the mean, and values become rarer the further you go from it, equally on both sides. This symmetric, bell-shaped pattern is the normal distribution (or Gaussian distribution).
A normal distribution is completely described by just two numbers: its mean (μ, where the peak is) and its standard deviation (σ, how wide the bell is).








dnorm() gives the height (density) of the normal curve, and stat_function() draws a function in a ggplot.

Real data: quiet standing force
Remember the quiet-standing phase before CMJ 3? Let’s look at the distribution of those 750 force samples, and overlay a normal curve with the same mean and SD:








(aes(y = after_stat(density)) scales the histogram so its total area is 1, like the curve.)
The fluctuations around body weight follow the normal curve quite closely. That’s typical for random noise: many small, independent influences (sway, breathing, electronic noise) adding up.


The 68–95–99.7 rule
For any normal distribution:

about 68 % of the values lie within 1 SD of the mean,
about 95 % lie within 2 SDs (more precisely 1.96),
about 99.7 % lie within 3 SDs.

This is why the onset threshold in lesson 2.3 used 5 SDs: if the force were just noise, a drop of more than 5 SDs would essentially never happen (less than 1 in a million samples).

Check the rule on the real data. Calculate the proportion of quiet-standing samples that lie within 1 SD of the mean (within_1sd) and within 2 SDs (within_2sd). Tip: abs() gives the absolute (positive) distance, and the mean() of a logical vector is the proportion of TRUEs.










Replace the blanks with s and 2 * s.




x <- quiet$force_total
m <- mean(x)
s <- sd(x)

# Proportion within 1 SD and within 2 SDs of the mean
within_1sd <- mean(abs(x - m) <= s)
within_2sd <- mean(abs(x - m) <= 2 * s)

within_1sd
within_2sd

title: 2.4 The normal distribution and the central limit theorem
text:
z-scores
A z-score tells you how many standard deviations a value lies above (+) or below (−) the mean:
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{SD}\]
z-scores are popular in sport science for athlete profiling, because they put very different tests (jump height in cm, sprint time in s, VO₂max in mL/kg/min) on the same scale. A z of +1.5 means “1.5 SDs better than the squad average”, whatever the test.
If the data are normal, you can turn a z-score into a percentile with pnorm(), the proportion of the normal distribution below a z-score:









A basketball squad’s CMJ heights are given. Calculate every player’s z-score and store the vector in z. Then select the names of the players with a z-score above +1 and store them in top_jumpers.

title: 2.4 The normal distribution and the central limit theorem
text:
Is my data normal?
Many statistical methods (t-tests, ANOVA, regression) assume that the data, or more exactly the errors, are approximately normal. Two graphical checks:

A histogram: is it roughly symmetric and bell-shaped?
A Q-Q plot (quantile–quantile plot): it plots the quantiles of your data against the quantiles of a normal distribution. If the data are normal, the points lie close to a straight line.

















Note that a Q-Q plot uses the aesthetic sample instead of x.

A jump-height test has a squad mean of 40 cm and SD of 4 cm (approximately normal). Roughly what percentage of players jump between 32 and 48 cm?

68 %
95 %
99.7 %


32 and 48 cm are 2 SDs below and above the mean (40 ± 2 × 4), so about 95 % of players lie between them.



A player’s sprint time has a z-score of −1.5 relative to the squad. What does that mean?

They are 1.5 s slower than average
Their time is 1.5 SDs below the squad mean, so they are one of the fastest
They are at the 15th percentile, so one of the slowest


A negative z means below the mean. For sprint times, lower is better, so z = −1.5 is fast. (Coaches often flip the sign for “lower is better” tests so that a positive z always means good.)

title: 2.4 The normal distribution and the central limit theorem
text:
The central limit theorem
Now for one of the most important ideas in all of statistics.
So far we’ve looked at the distribution of individual values. Now imagine you repeatedly take a sample of n values from a population and calculate the sample mean each time. Each sample gives a slightly different mean. How are these sample means distributed?






ImportantThe central limit theorem (CLT)



If you take many random samples of size n from any population (with mean μ and SD σ), then, provided n is large enough, the sample means:

are approximately normally distributed, even if the population itself is not normal,
are centred on the population mean μ,
have a standard deviation of \(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\), called the standard error (SE) of the mean.



A common rule of thumb is that n ≥ 30 is “large enough”, though for populations that aren’t very skewed, much smaller samples already work.

Seeing the CLT with a simulation
Let’s treat the 163 TMT-B times, which are strongly right-skewed, as our population, and simulate taking samples from it.
Two new functions:

sample(x, size = n, replace = TRUE) draws n random values from x,
replicate(1000, expression) repeats an expression 1000 times and collects the results.

set.seed() makes the random numbers reproducible: with the same seed you get the same “random” result every time.








Run the code with n <- 2, then change it to 5, 10, 30 and 60. What happens?

With small n, the sample means are still skewed, like the population.
As n grows, the histogram becomes a symmetric bell curve centred on the population mean (red line).
It also becomes narrower: larger samples give more precise means.

That narrowing is the standard error, σ/√n: to halve the SE, you need four times as many observations.


Using set.seed(42), simulate 1000 sample means with sample size n = 30 from population and store them in means_30.
Calculate the SD of these sample means (sd_of_means).
Calculate the theoretical standard error se = sd(population) / sqrt(30) and compare.












size = 30
sd(means_30)
sd(population) / sqrt(30)





population <- balance$tmt_b_s
set.seed(42)

# 1. 1000 means of samples of size 30
means_30 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(population, size = 30, replace = TRUE)))

# 2. SD of the sample means
sd_of_means <- sd(means_30)

# 3. Theoretical standard error
se <- sd(population) / sqrt(30)

sd_of_means
se
population <- balance$tmt_b_s
set.seed(42)

# 1. 1000 means of samples of size 30
means_30 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(population, size = 30, replace = TRUE)))

# 2. SD of the sample means
sd_of_means <- sd(means_30)

# 3. Theoretical standard error
se <- sd(population) / sqrt(30)

sd_of_means
se








Why the CLT matters to you

It’s the foundation of inferential statistics. Because sample means are approximately normal, we can calculate confidence intervals and run t-tests on means, even when the raw data aren’t perfectly normal (Module 4).
It explains why we average repeated trials. If a single jump varies with SD σ around an athlete’s “true” ability, the mean of 3 jumps varies with only σ/√3 ≈ 0.58σ. Averaging trials gives a more precise estimate. That’s why test protocols ask for several jumps.
It explains why the normal distribution is everywhere. Many biological measurements are the sum of many small, independent influences, and sums (like means) tend to be normal.


According to the CLT, what happens to the distribution of sample means as the sample size increases?

It becomes more skewed, like the population
It becomes more normal and narrower, centred on the population mean
It becomes wider


Sample means approach a normal distribution centred on μ, with a standard error σ/√n that shrinks as n grows.



The SD of single CMJ trials of an athlete is 1.2 cm. What is the standard error of the mean of 4 trials?

0.3 cm
0.6 cm
1.2 cm


SE = SD / √n = 1.2 / √4 = 1.2 / 2 = 0.6 cm.



Does the CLT say that your raw data become normal if you collect enough of it?

Yes, with n ≥ 30 the data are always normal
No, it’s about the distribution of sample means; the raw data keep their own shape (e.g. skewed)
Only if the data are continuous


A common misconception! Measuring 1000 TMT-B times still gives a skewed histogram. It’s the means of repeated samples that become normal.

title: 2.4 The normal distribution and the central limit theorem
text:
Lesson summary

The normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, defined by its mean and SD; ≈68 % / 95 % / 99.7 % of values lie within 1 / 2 / 3 SDs.
z = (x − mean) / SD puts different tests on a common scale; pnorm(z) converts it to a percentile for normal data.
Check normality with a histogram and a Q-Q plot (geom_qq() + geom_qq_line()).
Central limit theorem: means of samples of size n are approximately normal, centred on μ, with standard error σ/√n, whatever the shape of the population.

text:
Counting: geom_bar()

Values: geom_col()
If your data already contains the numbers you want as bar heights, use geom_col(), which needs both x and y. The typical case is a table of group means that you calculate first.
aggregate() calculates a statistic per group. The formula y ~ group means “y split by group”:









You want a bar chart showing how many athletes play each sport in squad. Which geom?

geom_bar() with aes(x = sport)
geom_col() with aes(x = sport)
geom_histogram() with aes(x = sport)

text:
Error bars: mean ± SD
A mean alone hides the variability. In sport science, group means are usually shown with error bars of ± 1 SD. Calculate the means and SDs first, then add geom_errorbar(), which needs the aesthetics ymin and ymax:








The width of geom_errorbar() sets the width of the little horizontal caps.

Make a bar chart of the mean body mass per sport, with error bars of ± 1 SD.

bm (means) is calculated for you. Add a column sd with the SDs.
Plot bm with geom_col() and geom_errorbar().











Use FUN = sd, and ymin = body_mass_kg - sd, ymax = body_mass_kg + sd.




bm <- aggregate(body_mass_kg ~ sport, data = squad, FUN = mean)

# 1. Add the SDs
bm$sd <- aggregate(body_mass_kg ~ sport, data = squad, FUN = sd)$body_mass_kg

# 2. Bars with error bars
