title: 3.1 Showing summaries and the data behind them
section: The problem with bar charts of means
text:
The problem with bar charts of means
Bar charts with error bars are so common that they have a nickname: dynamite plots. But for continuous data they are often a poor choice:

The bar suggests the data fill the whole area from 0 to the mean, which they don’t.
Very different datasets (a few outliers, two clusters, 5 or 500 athletes) can produce exactly the same bars.
Readers can’t see the sample size or the distribution.

Many journals now ask authors to show the individual data points. With ggplot2 that’s easy: draw the points, and add the summary on top with stat_summary(), which calculates the statistic for you.








The red point and bars are the same mean ± SD as before, but now you can also see every athlete. The basketball group has a few low jumpers, and the overlap between sports is large.
stat_summary() arguments:

fun: the function for the center (here mean),
fun.min / fun.max: functions for the lower and upper ends of the bar; function(x) mean(x) - sd(x) is a tiny function written on the spot,
geom: how to draw the result ("point", "errorbar", "pointrange", "col"…).


Show the peak power per kg (peak_power_rel) for each sport: the raw data with geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4), and the mean of each sport on top as a large point with stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "firebrick").










aes(x = sport, y = peak_power_rel), then geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) and stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "firebrick").




ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = peak_power_rel)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "firebrick")
ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = peak_power_rel)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "firebrick")







Why do many journals discourage bar charts of means for continuous data?

Bar charts can’t show error bars
They hide the distribution and sample size; very different datasets can produce identical bars
ggplot2 can’t draw them correctly


A bar shows one number (and the error bar maybe two). Showing the individual observations, with the mean ± SD on top, is more honest and informative, especially for the small samples typical in sport science.

title: 3.1 Showing summaries and the data behind them
section: Raw data + summary for several groups
text:
Raw data + summary for several groups
stat_summary() respects all the aesthetics you’ve learned. With colour mapped to a second variable and position_dodge(), you can compare subgroups. Here are Mini-BESTest scores by activity level and age group:









position_jitterdodge() both jitters and dodges the raw points,
geom = "pointrange" draws a point with a vertical line from ymin to ymax: a neat alternative to error bars.


Make the same type of plot for the squad data: jump height by sport, with the raw data as jittered points and the mean ± SD as a pointrange in red. Use geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) for the raw data.










fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x), fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x), geom = "pointrange".




ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean,
               fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x),
               fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x),
               geom = "pointrange", colour = "red", size = 0.8, linewidth = 1)
ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.4) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean,
               fun.min = function(x) mean(x) - sd(x),
               fun.max = function(x) mean(x) + sd(x),
               geom = "pointrange", colour = "red", size = 0.8, linewidth = 1)







What’s the difference between error bars showing ± SD and ± SE (standard error)?

SD shows how spread out the individual athletes are; SE shows how precisely the mean is estimated (SD / √n)
They are the same thing
SE is always larger than SD


SD describes the data; SE describes the uncertainty of the mean (lesson 2.4). SE error bars are √n times smaller, so always state in the caption which one you plotted!

text:
Lesson summary

geom_bar() counts rows per category; geom_col() plots values you calculated (e.g. with aggregate()).
position = "dodge" places bars side by side.
Error bars: geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ..., ymax = ...)).
Prefer raw data + summary: geom_jitter() + stat_summary(fun = mean, fun.min = ..., fun.max = ..., geom = "pointrange").
Always state whether error bars show SD, SE or a confidence interval.

title: 3.3 Scales, colours and labels
text:
What is a scale?
Every aesthetic (x, y, colour, fill, size, …) has a scale that translates data values into something visible: positions, colours or sizes. ggplot2 picks a sensible default scale, but you can override it by adding a scale_<aesthetic>_<type>() function:







Function
Controls




scale_x_continuous(), scale_y_continuous()
numeric axes


scale_x_discrete()
categorical axes (order, labels)


scale_colour_manual(), scale_fill_manual()
your own colours for categories


scale_colour_viridis_d(), scale_colour_viridis_c()
viridis palettes (discrete / continuous)


scale_x_log10()
logarithmic axis

title: 3.3 Scales, colours and labels
text:
Axes: breaks, limits and labels









breaks sets where the tick marks are,
labels changes how they’re written, e.g. labels = function(x) x * 100 to show metres as centimetres. The scales package (installed with ggplot2) has ready-made formatters such as scales::percent.


Zooming: limits vs. coord_cartesian()
There are two ways to zoom in, and they are not the same:

scale_y_continuous(limits = c(a, b)) removes all data outside the limits before any calculation,
coord_cartesian(ylim = c(a, b)) keeps all data and just zooms the view, like a camera.

The difference matters for anything ggplot2 calculates: box plots, smoothing lines, means. Compare:








The first plot gives a warning (“Removed … rows”) and its medians and boxes are wrong: they’re calculated only from the remaining athletes.

You want to zoom in on part of a scatter plot that has a regression line (geom_smooth(method = "lm")). What should you use?

scale_x_continuous(limits = ...)
coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)
Either: the result is identical


With limits, the points outside the range are removed and the regression line is refitted on fewer data, so it changes! coord_cartesian() only zooms the view.



Make a scatter plot of body_mass_kg (x) against jump_height_m (y), but show the y-axis in centimetres: use scale_y_continuous() with breaks = seq(0.25, 0.55, by = 0.05) and labels = function(x) x * 100. Label the axes with labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Jump height (cm)").










breaks = seq(0.25, 0.55, by = 0.05), labels = function(x) x * 100, and the axis titles from the task.




ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0.25, 0.55, by = 0.05), labels = function(x) x * 100) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Jump height (cm)")
ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0.25, 0.55, by = 0.05), labels = function(x) x * 100) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Jump height (cm)")

title: 3.3 Scales, colours and labels
text:
Colours

Choose colours for everyone
About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of colour-vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green. ggplot2’s default palette isn’t designed for this, and red/green combinations are the worst choice.
Two safe options:

The Okabe–Ito palette, designed to be distinguishable for all common types of colour blindness:










viridis palettes (scale_colour_viridis_d() for categories, scale_colour_viridis_c() for numbers), which are colour-blind friendly, print well in grey-scale and are perceptually uniform: equal steps in the data look like equal steps in colour.

scale_colour_manual(values = ...) assigns your own colours to the categories. A named vector makes sure each category always gets the same colour:








For a numeric variable mapped to colour, use a continuous viridis scale:








(\n starts a new line in a title.)

Make box plots of peak_power_rel per sport, with fill = sport. Colour the boxes with scale_fill_manual() using the named vector sport_cols (given), and hide the redundant legend with show.legend = FALSE in geom_boxplot().










show.legend = FALSE and scale_fill_manual(values = sport_cols). Use the fill version because the boxes use fill.




sport_cols <- c(Basketball = "#E69F00", Soccer = "#0072B2")

ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = peak_power_rel, fill = sport)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sport_cols)
sport_cols <- c(Basketball = "#E69F00", Soccer = "#0072B2")

ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = peak_power_rel, fill = sport)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sport_cols)







Which colour combination should you avoid for two groups?

Red and green
Orange and blue
Black and light grey


Red–green colour-vision deficiency is by far the most common type. Orange/blue (as in Okabe–Ito) is a safe pair.

title: 3.3 Scales, colours and labels
text:
Ordering categories
Categories appear in alphabetical order by default. For ordinal data that’s wrong, and for nominal data a meaningful order (e.g. by the median) makes plots easier to read. Change the order by setting the factor levels (lesson 1.3), or use reorder() to sort categories by a statistic:

title: 3.3 Scales, colours and labels
text:
Labels with units
Every axis title of a scientific figure should state the quantity and its unit: “Jump height (cm)”, not “jump_height_m”. labs() sets all titles in one go:








You can transform data directly inside aes(): y = jump_height_m * 100 plots centimetres without changing the data frame.
For special notation, R understands plotmath expressions: labs(y = expression("Force (N·kg"^-1*")")) gives a superscript. Plain text such as “N/kg” or Unicode characters (“m·s⁻¹”) are often simpler.

Complete the plot of con_time_s (x) against con_force_rel (y), coloured by jump_height_m with scale_colour_viridis_c(). Add labels: x = "Propulsion time (s)", y = "Mean propulsive force (N/kg)", colour = "Jump height (m)".










scale_colour_viridis_c(), then the three labels exactly as given in the task.




ggplot(squad, aes(x = con_time_s, y = con_force_rel, colour = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = "Propulsion time (s)", y = "Mean propulsive force (N/kg)", colour = "Jump height (m)")
ggplot(squad, aes(x = con_time_s, y = con_force_rel, colour = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = "Propulsion time (s)", y = "Mean propulsive force (N/kg)", colour = "Jump height (m)")







Which axis title is best for a scientific figure?

peak_power_rel
Power
Peak power (W/kg)


A good axis title names the quantity in words and gives its unit. Column names are for code, not for readers.

Zoom with coord_cartesian(); limits deletes data and changes computed statistics.

title: 3.5 Force–time curves and multi-panel figures
section: The problem: trials don’t start at the same time
text:
The problem: trials don’t start at the same time
Let’s overlay Athlete K’s three jumps:








The recordings started at different moments before each jump, so the curves are shifted and hard to compare. The solution is to align the trials to a common event. Take-off is easy to detect: it’s the first sample where the force drops below a small threshold (20 N).

Aligning to take-off
First find the take-off time of each trial. tapply() applies a function per group, and the function can be one you write on the spot:








takeoff is a named vector, so takeoff["CMJ 2"] gives the take-off time of CMJ 2, and takeoff[cmj$trial] gives the take-off time of the matching trial for every row. Subtracting it creates a time axis where 0 = take-off:









Plot the aligned trials: time_rel (x) against force_total (y), one coloured line per trial. Zoom in on the interval from −1.2 s to 0.8 s with coord_cartesian(), and add a dashed vertical line at take-off (geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed")).










x = time_rel, colour = trial, xintercept = 0, xlim = c(-1.2, 0.8).




takeoff <- tapply(cmj$time_s[cmj$force_total < 20], cmj$trial[cmj$force_total < 20], min)
cmj$time_rel <- cmj$time_s - takeoff[cmj$trial]

ggplot(cmj, aes(x = time_rel, y = force_total, colour = trial)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1.2, 0.8))
takeoff <- tapply(cmj$time_s[cmj$force_total < 20], cmj$trial[cmj$force_total < 20], min)
cmj$time_rel <- cmj$time_s - takeoff[cmj$trial]

ggplot(cmj, aes(x = time_rel, y = force_total, colour = trial)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-1.2, 0.8))

title: 3.5 Force–time curves and multi-panel figures
text:
Normalising to body weight
Forces are often expressed in multiples of body weight (BW), which makes athletes of different sizes comparable and makes the curve easier to read: 1 BW = standing still, 0 = flight. Athlete K’s body weight is ≈ 726 N (lesson 2.2):

title: 3.5 Force–time curves and multi-panel figures
section: Wide vs. long data: left and right legs
text:
Wide vs. long data: left and right legs
cmj stores the two legs in two columns (force_left, force_right). That’s called wide format. ggplot2 wants long format instead: one column with the force and one column saying which leg it belongs to. Then you can simply map colour = leg.
You can build the long data by stacking two data frames with rbind():








(The tidyr package’s pivot_longer() does this in one step, which is very useful once you have many columns.)

Build legs for CMJ 1 (as above) and plot the left and right force over time as two coloured lines. Shade the flight phase with annotate("rect", ...): in CMJ 1 the flight lasts from about 4.58 s to 5.16 s. Use ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf so the shading covers the full height, with alpha = 0.2.










force_left and force_right; colour = leg; xmin = 4.58, xmax = 5.16.




cmj1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1")

legs <- rbind(
  data.frame(time_s = cmj1$time_s, leg = "Left",  force = cmj1$force_left),
  data.frame(time_s = cmj1$time_s, leg = "Right", force = cmj1$force_right)
)

ggplot(legs, aes(x = time_s, y = force, colour = leg)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 4.58, xmax = 5.16, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Vertical force (N)")
cmj1 <- subset(cmj, trial == "CMJ 1")

legs <- rbind(
  data.frame(time_s = cmj1$time_s, leg = "Left",  force = cmj1$force_left),
  data.frame(time_s = cmj1$time_s, leg = "Right", force = cmj1$force_right)
)

ggplot(legs, aes(x = time_s, y = force, colour = leg)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 4.58, xmax = 5.16, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Vertical force (N)")







Why do we align repeated trials to take-off before overlaying them?

To make the recordings shorter
Because recordings start at arbitrary moments, so the same movement phase happens at different clock times in each trial
Because ggplot2 can’t plot different time ranges


Time since the start of the recording has no biomechanical meaning. Aligning to a clear event (onset, take-off, foot contact) makes the phases comparable across trials and athletes.



You have a data frame with columns time, hr_athlete1, hr_athlete2, hr_athlete3. To plot one coloured line per athlete with ggplot2, you should first…

add three geom_line() layers, one per column
reshape it to long format: columns time, athlete, hr
calculate the mean of the three columns


Three separate layers works, but it doesn’t scale and you lose the automatic legend. Long (“tidy”) data, with one row per observation, is what ggplot2 is designed for.

title: 3.5 Force–time curves and multi-panel figures
text:
Combining plots with patchwork
Journal figures often have several panels (A, B, C…). The patchwork package lets you combine ggplot objects with simple operators:







Code
Layout




p1 + p2 or p1 | p2
side by side


p1 / p2
on top of each other


(p1 | p2) / p3
two on top, one below


+ plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
add panel tags A, B, C


+ plot_layout(guides = "collect")
combine duplicate legends into one











Together, the three panels tell a story: soccer players jump slightly higher (A), but they are also much lighter (C), and lighter athletes tend to jump higher (B). Is it the sport or the body mass? You’ll answer that with multiple regression in Module 4.

Combine the two plots p_force and p_power (given) side by side, with panel tags A and B, and with their two identical legends collected into one.










(p_force | p_power), tag_levels = "A", guides = "collect". The brackets matter: + is evaluated before |, so without them the annotation would be added to p_power only.




p_force <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = con_force_rel, y = jump_height_m, colour = sport)) +
  geom_point() + scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Mean propulsive force (N/kg)", y = "Jump height (m)", colour = NULL)

p_power <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = peak_power_rel, y = jump_height_m, colour = sport)) +
  geom_point() + scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Peak power (W/kg)", y = "Jump height (m)", colour = NULL)

(p_force | p_power) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")
p_force <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = con_force_rel, y = jump_height_m, colour = sport)) +
  geom_point() + scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Mean propulsive force (N/kg)", y = "Jump height (m)", colour = NULL)

p_power <- ggplot(squad, aes(x = peak_power_rel, y = jump_height_m, colour = sport)) +
  geom_point() + scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols) +
  labs(x = "Peak power (W/kg)", y = "Jump height (m)", colour = NULL)

(p_force | p_power) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")

title: 4.1 Sampling and confidence intervals
text:
From descriptive to inferential statistics
In Module 2 you described data. Now we want to generalise. The squad dataset contains 42 professional soccer players. Their mean jump height is a statistic. What we really want to know is the parameter: the mean jump height of all professional soccer players of this level.








If we had tested 42 other soccer players, we would have found a slightly different mean. This sampling variability is why an estimate always needs a measure of its uncertainty.

title: 4.1 Sampling and confidence intervals
text:
The standard error
You met the standard error in lesson 2.4: it’s the standard deviation of the sample means you would get if you repeated the study many times. You can estimate it from a single sample:
\[SE = \frac{SD}{\sqrt{n}}\]

title: 4.1 Sampling and confidence intervals
text:
Confidence intervals
A 95 % confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the population mean:
\[\bar{x} \pm t^* \times SE\]
where \(t^*\) is a value from the t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom. The t-distribution looks like the normal distribution but has heavier tails, which accounts for the extra uncertainty of estimating the SD from a small sample. For large samples \(t^*\) is close to the familiar 1.96. You get it with qt():








(0.975 because 2.5 % is cut off in each tail, leaving 95 % in the middle.)

Calculate the 95 % CI of the mean jump height of the soccer players by hand.

Calculate m (mean), se (standard error) and t_star (with qt(), df = n − 1).
Calculate lower and upper.











m <- mean(x), se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n), t_star <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1), lower <- m - t_star * se, upper <- m + t_star * se.




soccer <- subset(squad, sport == "Soccer")
x <- soccer$jump_height_m
n <- length(x)

# 1. Ingredients
m <- mean(x)
se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)
t_star <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)

# 2. The interval
lower <- m - t_star * se
upper <- m + t_star * se
c(lower, upper)
soccer <- subset(squad, sport == "Soccer")

n <- length(x)

# 1. Ingredients

se <- sd(x) / sqrt(n)

# 2. The interval

upper <- m + t_star * se
c(lower, upper)






R does all of this in one step with t.test(). The CI is part of its output, and you can extract it with $conf.int:

title: 4.1 Sampling and confidence intervals
text:
What does “95 % confidence” mean?
This is subtle and often misunderstood. The population mean is a fixed (unknown) number; it’s the interval that varies from sample to sample. The correct interpretation:

If we repeated the study many times and calculated a 95 % CI each time, about 95 % of those intervals would contain the true population mean.

A simulation makes this concrete. Let’s pretend we know the truth: jump heights in a population are normal with mean 40 cm and SD 5 cm. We draw 50 samples of 15 athletes and compute a CI from each:








rnorm(n, mean, sd) draws random numbers from a normal distribution, and the for loop repeats the code for i = 1, 2, …, 50. Most intervals (grey) contain the true mean of 40 cm; a few (red) miss it. Run the code with another seed to see that it’s about 95 % in the long run.

A study reports “mean jump height 40.6 cm, 95 % CI 39.0 to 42.1 cm”. Which interpretation is correct?

95 % of the players jump between 39.0 and 42.1 cm
There is a 95 % probability that the true mean lies in this specific interval
The interval was produced by a method that captures the true population mean in 95 % of studies; values in the interval are plausible values for that mean


The first statement confuses the CI of the mean with the spread of individual values (that would be roughly mean ± 2 SD). The second is a very common shortcut; strictly, the true mean is either in the interval or not. The probability belongs to the method, not to one interval.

title: 4.1 Sampling and confidence intervals
text:
What makes a CI narrow?
The width of a CI is \(2 \times t^* \times SD / \sqrt{n}\), so a CI gets narrower when:

the sample size n increases (but slowly: 4× the athletes for half the width),
the variability (SD) is smaller, e.g. thanks to a more reliable test,
you accept less confidence (a 90 % CI is narrower than a 95 % CI).


Compare the precision of the estimates for the two sports. Use t.test() to get the 95 % CI of the mean body mass of the basketball players (ci_basket) and of the soccer players (ci_soccer). Then calculate the width of each CI (upper − lower, use diff()).










t.test(basket$body_mass_kg)$conf.int and the same for soccer.




basket <- subset(squad, sport == "Basketball")
soccer <- subset(squad, sport == "Soccer")

ci_basket <- t.test(basket$body_mass_kg)$conf.int
ci_soccer <- t.test(soccer$body_mass_kg)$conf.int

# Widths
diff(ci_basket)
diff(ci_soccer)
basket <- subset(squad, sport == "Basketball")
soccer <- subset(squad, sport == "Soccer")

ci_basket <- t.test(basket$body_mass_kg)$conf.int
ci_soccer <- t.test(soccer$body_mass_kg)$conf.int

# Widths
diff(ci_basket)
diff(ci_soccer)







You want to halve the width of a confidence interval. Roughly how many more athletes do you need?

Twice as many
Four times as many
Ten times as many


The width is proportional to 1/√n. To halve it, √n must double, so n must be 4 times larger.



In a paper, two groups’ means are plotted with error bars that don’t say what they are. Why is that a problem?

It isn’t: all error bars mean the same
SD, SE and 95 % CI bars have very different sizes and meanings; the reader can’t interpret the figure
Error bars should never be used


For n = 42, the 95 % CI is about 2 × SE, and SD bars are √42 ≈ 6.5 times larger than SE bars. The caption must say which one is shown.

title: 4.1 Sampling and confidence intervals
text:
Lesson summary

A sample statistic estimates a population parameter; the SE = SD / √n quantifies its precision.
95 % CI = mean ± t* × SE, with t* = qt(0.975, df = n - 1). Shortcut: t.test(x)$conf.int.
Interpretation: 95 % of CIs constructed this way contain the true value.
Narrower CIs come from larger samples and less variability.

title: 4.3 Comparing two groups
text:
Independent vs. paired designs








Design
Example
Test




Independent groups: different athletes in each group
basketball vs. soccer players
independent t-test


Paired / repeated measures: the same athletes measured twice
jump height before vs. after a training block; left vs. right leg
paired t-test



Choosing the right one matters: paired designs remove the (often large) differences between athletes, so they can detect smaller effects with fewer participants.

title: 4.3 Comparing two groups
text:
The independent t-test
Do soccer and basketball players differ in jump height? Always plot first:








H₀: the population means are equal (difference = 0). Use t.test() with a formula outcome ~ group:








Reading the output:

t = −2.05 on about 79 degrees of freedom, p = 0.044,
the 95 % CI of the difference (basketball − soccer) runs from −4.8 to −0.07 cm,
the group means are 0.381 m and 0.406 m.

So soccer players jump on average 2.5 cm higher, and the difference is (just) statistically significant.






TipWelch or Student?



R’s default is the Welch t-test, which doesn’t assume equal variances in the two groups. The classic Student t-test (var.equal = TRUE) does. Welch is the safer default and loses almost nothing when variances are equal, so keep the default.



Do basketball and soccer players differ in relative peak power (peak_power_rel)? Run an independent (Welch) t-test and store it in res. Then extract the 95 % CI of the difference (res$conf.int).










t.test(peak_power_rel ~ sport, data = squad)




res <- t.test(peak_power_rel ~ sport, data = squad)
res
res$conf.int
res <- t.test(peak_power_rel ~ sport, data = squad)
res
res$conf.int

title: 4.3 Comparing two groups
text:
Effect size: Cohen’s d
The p-value tells you whether a difference is detectable, not how large it is. Cohen’s d expresses the difference in units of standard deviation:
\[d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{SD_{pooled}}, \qquad SD_{pooled} = \sqrt{\frac{SD_1^2 + SD_2^2}{2}}\]
(this simple pooled SD is correct when the groups have the same size). Conventional benchmarks: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. In sport science, also compare the raw difference with the smallest worthwhile change (lesson 4.9).

Calculate Cohen’s d for the difference in jump height between soccer and basketball players (soccer − basketball).










sd_pooled <- sqrt((sd(b)^2 + sd(s)^2) / 2) (var(b) is the same as sd(b)^2), then divide by sd_pooled.




b <- squad$jump_height_m[squad$sport == "Basketball"]
s <- squad$jump_height_m[squad$sport == "Soccer"]

sd_pooled <- sqrt((sd(b)^2 + sd(s)^2) / 2)
d <- (mean(s) - mean(b)) / sd_pooled
d
b <- squad$jump_height_m[squad$sport == "Basketball"]
s <- squad$jump_height_m[squad$sport == "Soccer"]

sd_pooled <- sqrt((sd(b)^2 + sd(s)^2) / 2)
d <- (mean(s) - mean(b)) / sd_pooled
d







Two studies compare the same training methods. Study A (n = 400) finds p = 0.001, d = 0.15. Study B (n = 20) finds p = 0.09, d = 0.70. Which statement is correct?

Study A found the bigger effect
Study B observed a larger effect, but with so few participants it’s estimated imprecisely
Study B shows there is no effect


p mixes effect size and sample size. Study A’s effect is small but precisely estimated; study B’s is larger but uncertain (wide CI).

title: 4.3 Comparing two groups
text:
The paired t-test
The trials data contains three CMJs per athlete (56 athletes), performed one after the other in the same session:








Do athletes jump higher in their third trial than in their first (a warm-up or learning effect)? These are the same athletes, so the measurements are paired. A paired t-test is a one-sample t-test on the differences: H₀ says the mean difference is 0.
First, put trial 1 and trial 3 next to each other. Because trials is sorted by athlete, the athletes are in the same order in both vectors:









Run a paired t-test comparing t3 and t1 (t.test(t3, t1, paired = TRUE)) and store it in res. Then check that it equals a one-sample t-test on the differences: t.test(t3 - t1)$p.value.










t.test(t3, t1, paired = TRUE)




t1 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 1]
t3 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 3]

res <- t.test(t3, t1, paired = TRUE)
res

# Same thing:
t.test(t3 - t1)$p.value
t1 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 1]
t3 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 3]

res <- t.test(t3, t1, paired = TRUE)
res

# Same thing:
t.test(t3 - t1)$p.value







Why pairing matters
What if you wrongly treated the same data as two independent groups?








The difference between athletes (some jump 30 cm, others 50 cm) is much larger than the change between trials. The independent test treats that between-athlete variation as noise, so it has much less power. The paired test removes it by looking only at within-athlete changes.

You measure hamstring strength of the left and right legs of 25 footballers. Which test compares the legs?

Independent t-test
Paired t-test
One-sample t-test against 0 N


Both legs belong to the same athlete, so the measurements are paired. (Technically it’s a one-sample t-test on the left − right differences, which is exactly what a paired t-test does.)

title: 4.3 Comparing two groups
text:
Assumptions and alternatives
t-tests assume that the data (or for paired tests, the differences) are roughly normally distributed, and that observations are independent (each athlete appears once per group). Thanks to the central limit theorem, t-tests are robust to moderate non-normality when samples aren’t tiny. Check with a histogram or Q-Q plot (lesson 2.4).
For clearly skewed data, small samples or ordinal outcomes, use the non-parametric alternatives, which work on ranks:

independent groups: Mann–Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum test, wilcox.test(y ~ group, data = ...),
paired data: Wilcoxon signed-rank test, wilcox.test(x, y, paired = TRUE).










Which situation calls most clearly for wilcox.test() instead of t.test()?

80 athletes per group, jump heights roughly normal
9 patients per group, pain scores on a 0–10 scale with many zeros
Body mass of 40 men and 40 women


A small sample with an ordinal, heavily skewed outcome is where rank-based tests are most appropriate.

title: 4.3 Comparing two groups
text:
Lesson summary

Independent groups: t.test(y ~ group, data = df) (Welch by default).
Paired data: t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE), equivalent to a one-sample test of the differences.
Always report the mean difference with its 95 % CI and an effect size such as Cohen’s d = difference / pooled SD.
Non-parametric alternatives: wilcox.test() (unpaired or paired = TRUE).


Scratchpad
squad, trials and balance are loaded.

title: 4.5 Correlation
text:
Pearson’s correlation coefficient
The correlation coefficient r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two numeric variables:

r = +1: perfect positive linear relationship,
r = 0: no linear relationship,
r = −1: perfect negative linear relationship.









cor(x, y) gives r; cor.test(x, y) also gives a p-value (H₀: r = 0 in the population) and a 95 % CI:









r² = shared variance
Squaring r gives the proportion of variance that the two variables share. Peak power and jump height have r = 0.83, so r² = 0.69: 69 % of the variability in jump height is shared with peak power. Mean propulsive force (r = 0.31) shares only r² = 10 %.
Rough guide for |r| in sport science: < 0.1 trivial, 0.1–0.3 small, 0.3–0.5 moderate, 0.5–0.7 large, 0.7–0.9 very large, > 0.9 nearly perfect. But as you’ll see below, how two variables were obtained matters more than the size of r.

Test the correlation between contraction time (contraction_time_s) and jump height. Store the test in res, and calculate the shared variance r2 from res$estimate.










cor.test(squad$contraction_time_s, squad$jump_height_m), and r2 <- res$estimate^2.




res <- cor.test(squad$contraction_time_s, squad$jump_height_m)
res

r2 <- res$estimate^2
r2
res <- cor.test(squad$contraction_time_s, squad$jump_height_m)
res

r2 <- res$estimate^2
r2

title: 4.5 Correlation
text:
Pearson or Spearman?
Pearson’s r assumes a linear relationship and is sensitive to outliers. Spearman’s ρ (rho) correlates the ranks of the values instead, so it captures any monotonic relationship (consistently increasing or decreasing) and is robust to outliers. It’s also the right choice for ordinal data.

title: 4.5 Correlation
section: When a high correlation tells you nothing new: mathematical coupling
text:
When a high correlation tells you nothing new: mathematical coupling
Here is the most important idea in this lesson. A force platform produces dozens of variables from one force–time curve: jump height, take-off velocity, impulse, power, RSI… They are not independent measurements. Many are calculated from each other or are linked by the laws of physics. Correlating them can produce impressive r values that reflect definitions and physics, not physiology.

Case 1: one variable calculated from the other
Jump height h is calculated from the take-off velocity vTO (or vice versa) with the projectile equation:
\[h = \frac{v_{TO}^2}{2g} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_{TO} = \sqrt{2 g h}\]
So if you know one, you know the other exactly. Their “correlation” is just the curvature of a square-root function:








r = 0.999. Reporting “take-off velocity was very strongly correlated with jump height (r = 0.999, p < 0.001)” would be a correlation of a variable with itself. They contain the same variance.


Case 2: two routes to the same physical quantity
The impulse–momentum theorem (Newton’s second law integrated over time) says that the net impulse applied during propulsion equals the change in momentum:
\[J_{net} = \int (F - mg)\,dt = m \cdot v_{TO} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{J_{net}}{m} = v_{TO}\]
In words: net impulse per kg is the take-off velocity, expressed in different units (N·s/kg = m/s). In the squad data, con_impulse_rel is the propulsive impulse per kg including the part that just supports body weight, so the net impulse per kg is:
\[\frac{J_{net}}{m} = \text{con\_impulse\_rel} - g \times \text{con\_time\_s}\]


Calculate the take-off velocity v_to from jump height.
Calculate the net propulsive impulse per kg net_imp from con_impulse_rel and con_time_s.
Calculate the correlation between net_imp and v_to (r_physics), and between the gross impulse con_impulse_rel and v_to (r_gross).












sqrt(2 * g * squad$jump_height_m)
squad$con_impulse_rel - g * squad$con_time_s
cor(squad$net_imp, squad$v_to) and cor(squad$con_impulse_rel, squad$v_to)





g <- 9.81

# 1. Take-off velocity from jump height (m/s)
squad$v_to <- sqrt(2 * g * squad$jump_height_m)

# 2. Net propulsive impulse per kg (N·s/kg)
squad$net_imp <- squad$con_impulse_rel - g * squad$con_time_s

# 3. Correlations
r_physics <- cor(squad$net_imp, squad$v_to)
r_gross <- cor(squad$con_impulse_rel, squad$v_to)
c(r_physics = r_physics, r_gross = r_gross)
g <- 9.81

# 1. Take-off velocity from jump height (m/s)
squad$v_to <- sqrt(2 * g * squad$jump_height_m)

# 2. Net propulsive impulse per kg (N·s/kg)
squad$net_imp <- squad$con_impulse_rel - g * squad$con_time_s

# 3. Correlations
r_physics <- cor(squad$net_imp, squad$v_to)
r_gross <- cor(squad$con_impulse_rel, squad$v_to)
c(r_physics = r_physics, r_gross = r_gross)






Plot it against the identity line:








The points scatter tightly around the identity line. So what does r = 0.96 mean here?

It does not mean “athletes who produce more impulse jump higher” as a physiological discovery. That’s Newton’s second law, true for every object.
It does tell you how well two calculation methods agree. The ~4 % of non-shared variance is measurement error and processing differences (how take-off and movement onset are detected, sampling rate, flight-time vs. impulse methods). In that sense, it’s a check of data quality, like the identity-line check in lesson 3.2.







ImportantThe take-home message



When two variables are two expressions of the same quantity (h and vTO, net impulse/mass and vTO), they share almost all of their variance by definition. Their correlation will be close to 1 no matter which athletes you test. It answers no research question about performance, and it should never be presented as a “finding”.




Case 3: partly shared components
Coupling isn’t always complete. Many derived variables share an ingredient:








Variable
Calculated as
Shares an ingredient with




Power
force × velocity
take-off velocity, and therefore jump height


RSImod
jump height / contraction time
jump height (numerator) and contraction time (denominator)


Relative impulse, force, power
value / body mass
body mass (denominator)



The correlation between RSImod and jump height (r = 0.66) is partly built in, because jump height is in RSImod. A simulation shows that this happens even with completely random, unrelated numbers:

Simulate 1000 “athletes” whose jump height h and contraction time t are independent random numbers. Then calculate the ratio rsi <- h / t and its correlations with h and with t.










rsi <- h / t, cor(rsi, h), cor(rsi, t).




set.seed(10)
h <- rnorm(1000, mean = 0.40, sd = 0.05)   # jump height (m)
t <- rnorm(1000, mean = 0.80, sd = 0.10)   # contraction time (s), unrelated to h

rsi <- h / t

r_h_t   <- cor(h, t)      # independent: close to 0
r_rsi_h <- cor(rsi, h)
r_rsi_t <- cor(rsi, t)
round(c(r_h_t = r_h_t, r_rsi_h = r_rsi_h, r_rsi_t = r_rsi_t), 2)
set.seed(10)
h <- rnorm(1000, mean = 0.40, sd = 0.05)   # jump height (m)
t <- rnorm(1000, mean = 0.80, sd = 0.10)   # contraction time (s), unrelated to h

rsi <- h / t

r_h_t   <- cor(h, t)      # independent: close to 0
r_rsi_h <- cor(rsi, h)
r_rsi_t <- cor(rsi, t)
round(c(r_h_t = r_h_t, r_rsi_h = r_rsi_h, r_rsi_t = r_rsi_t), 2)






The same trap applies to ratio scaling by body mass: dividing by mass doesn’t necessarily remove the effect of size, and can even create a correlation with mass. In the squad, relative propulsive impulse (per kg) still correlates negatively with body mass:








Heavier athletes look “worse” per kg. Part of this is real physiology, but part is an artefact of dividing by mass when impulse doesn’t scale 1:1 with mass. Allometric scaling (dividing by mass raised to a power estimated from the data, e.g. m0.67) is the solution; you’ll fit such a model with log-transformed regression in the next lesson’s exercises.

A paper reports that “peak velocity was strongly related to jump height (r = 0.95)” in a group of volleyball players. What’s your critical comment?

The sample was probably too small
Jump height is largely determined by take-off velocity, which is closely linked to peak velocity, so the variables share most of their variance by definition; this is physics, not a finding about volleyball players
Spearman’s rho should have been used


When variables are mathematically or physically coupled, a high r is expected for any group of people, or even for a bouncing ball. Such correlations can validate a measurement method, but not a training hypothesis.



Which pair of variables is least affected by mathematical coupling?

RSImod and jump height
Net impulse per kg and take-off velocity
Body mass and countermovement depth


RSImod contains jump height, and net impulse/mass equals take-off velocity by Newton’s law. Body mass and countermovement depth are measured independently, so any correlation between them reflects a genuine association (whatever its cause).

title: 4.5 Correlation
text:
Correlation is not causation
Even when variables are measured independently, a correlation doesn’t show that one causes the other. Body mass correlates negatively with jump height (r = −0.37), but body mass also differs between the sports, and the sports differ in training, selection and playing demands. A third variable (a confounder) can create or hide a correlation. Multiple regression (lesson 4.7) lets you adjust for confounders, but only randomised experiments can establish causation convincingly.

title: 4.5 Correlation
text:
A correlation matrix
cor() on a data frame of numeric columns gives all pairwise correlations at once:








When you read such a matrix, ask for every large value: are these two independent measurements, or do they share an ingredient?

r = −0.70 between countermovement depth (cmj_depth_m, negative = deeper) and propulsion time. What does r² tell you?

70 % of athletes have a deep countermovement
Depth and propulsion time share about 49 % of their variance
Deeper squats cause 70 % longer propulsion


r² = 0.70² = 0.49. (The negative sign only means that more negative depth, i.e. deeper, goes with longer propulsion: a longer distance to push over.)

title: 4.5 Correlation
text:
Lesson summary

cor(x, y) and cor.test(x, y): Pearson’s r; method = "spearman" for ranks/monotonic/outliers.
r² = shared variance.
Mathematical coupling: variables calculated from each other (h ↔︎ vTO), or two routes to the same physical quantity (net impulse/mass = vTO), share their variance by definition, so r ≈ 1 is not a finding. Ratios (RSI, per-kg values) create partial, built-in correlations.
Correlation ≠ causation: beware of confounders.


Scratchpad

title: 4.7 Multiple regression
text:
The model
Multiple regression extends the straight line to several predictors:
\[y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_k x_k + \varepsilon\]
In R, you simply add predictors to the formula with +:
lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = df)
The crucial change in interpretation: b₁ is the expected change in y for a 1-unit increase in x₁, while all other predictors are held constant. This is called the adjusted (or partial) effect.

title: 4.7 Multiple regression
text:
Part 1 · Adjusting for a confounder
In lesson 4.3, soccer players jumped 2.5 cm higher than basketball players (p = 0.044). But they’re also 20 kg lighter, and lighter athletes jump higher. Body mass is a potential confounder: it’s related to both the “exposure” (sport) and the outcome (jump height).









A categorical predictor
First, the sport-only model:








R turns the factor sport into a dummy variable: sportSoccer is 1 for soccer players and 0 for basketball players. The first level alphabetically (Basketball) is the reference. So:

Intercept (0.381 m) = mean jump height of the reference group (basketball),
sportSoccer (0.025 m) = difference soccer − basketball. That’s the same 2.5 cm and the same p as the t-test!

(A t-test is just a regression with one binary predictor.)

Fit a model with both sport and body_mass_kg as predictors of jump height. Store it in model_adj and extract the coefficient table coefs with summary(model_adj)$coefficients.










lm(jump_height_m ~ sport + body_mass_kg, data = squad)




model_adj <- lm(jump_height_m ~ sport + body_mass_kg, data = squad)
coefs <- summary(model_adj)$coefficients
round(coefs, 4)
model_adj <- lm(jump_height_m ~ sport + body_mass_kg, data = squad)
coefs <- summary(model_adj)$coefficients
round(coefs, 4)






Interpretation: “Soccer players jump higher” was largely explained by them being lighter. Comparing a basketball and a soccer player of the same body mass, the model predicts almost no difference. The sport effect was confounded by body mass.
You can visualise the adjusted model: it’s two parallel lines, one per sport, with the same slope for body mass:














WarningAdjustment is not magic



Regression can only adjust for confounders you measured, and only as well as the model fits. There’s also an overlap problem here: almost no basketball players are as light as most soccer players (lesson 4.4), so “the same body mass” is partly an extrapolation. Observational data can suggest, but rarely prove, causal effects.



In lm(jump_height_m ~ sport + body_mass_kg), how do you interpret the body-mass coefficient of −0.0017 m/kg?

Every kg of body mass reduces jump height by 0.17 cm in every athlete
Among athletes of the same sport, each additional kg goes with 0.17 cm lower jump height on average
Body mass explains 17 % of jump height


It’s an average, adjusted (partial) association, holding sport constant. It isn’t a causal effect for an individual, and not a proportion of variance.

title: 4.7 Multiple regression
section: Part 2 · Two weak predictors, one strong model
text:
Part 2 · Two weak predictors, one strong model
Here’s a puzzle. Physics says that take-off velocity comes from the net impulse, i.e. the average net force multiplied by the time it acts (lesson 4.5). So both mean propulsive force and propulsion time should matter. But look at them one by one:








Only 10 % and 5 % of the variance explained! Now look at how the two predictors relate to each other:








r = −0.83: a strong trade-off. Athletes who push off quickly produce high forces; athletes with long push-offs produce lower forces. Each strategy can lead to a high jump. That’s why each variable alone says little about jump height: a high force usually comes with a short time, and vice versa. Only by knowing both can you tell how big the impulse was.

Fit model_ft, predicting jump height from both con_force_rel and con_time_s, and extract its R² (r2_ft).










lm(jump_height_m ~ con_force_rel + con_time_s, data = squad)




model_ft <- lm(jump_height_m ~ con_force_rel + con_time_s, data = squad)
summary(model_ft)

r2_ft <- summary(model_ft)$r.squared
r2_ft
model_ft <- lm(jump_height_m ~ con_force_rel + con_time_s, data = squad)
summary(model_ft)

r2_ft <- summary(model_ft)$r.squared
r2_ft






This phenomenon, where adding a predictor increases the importance of another, is called suppression. It happens when predictors are correlated with each other in the opposite direction to their effects on the outcome. It’s a powerful reminder that simple correlations can be misleading when predictors are related.

Interactions: when effects multiply
Physics says velocity = (force − g) × time: the effects multiply rather than add. A model with + assumes the force effect is the same at every propulsion time. An interaction term lets the effect of one predictor depend on the other. In R, x1 * x2 means x1 + x2 + x1:x2 (both main effects plus their product):








R² rises from 0.87 to 0.95. And what’s left over (5 %) is mostly measurement and processing noise, plus the fact that h depends on v² rather than v.






ImportantRemember mathematical coupling



Why can force and time explain 95 % of jump height? Because jump height is calculated from the same force–time curve: force × time is impulse, and impulse is take-off velocity. This model is a nice demonstration of physics and of a force–time strategy trade-off, but it’s not a discovery that “force and time determine jumping ability”. They define it.
The informative questions are about the strategy: which athletes rely on force, which on time, and does that relate to sport, injury or training? Avoid putting variables like take-off velocity, net impulse or power into a model predicting jump height: you’d just be predicting jump height from itself.



Mean propulsive force alone explains 10 % of jump height, propulsion time alone 5 %, and both together 87 %. What’s the best explanation?

A calculation error
Force and time are strongly negatively correlated (a trade-off); together they reconstruct the impulse that determines take-off velocity
Adding predictors always increases R² by a lot


This is suppression. Adding any predictor increases R² a little, but a jump from 0.10 to 0.87 only happens because the second predictor corrects the first.

title: 4.7 Multiple regression
text:
Part 3 · Choosing between models
Adding predictors always increases R² a little, even if the new predictor is pure noise. To compare models fairly:

Adjusted R² penalises for the number of predictors; it only increases if a new predictor helps more than chance would.
AIC (Akaike information criterion): lower is better; also balances fit and complexity.
anova(model_small, model_big): an F-test of whether the extra predictors in a nested model (the big one contains all predictors of the small one) significantly improve the fit.


Does countermovement depth (cmj_depth_m) add information beyond force and time?

Fit m1 (force + time) and m2 (force + time + depth).
Compare them with anova(m1, m2) and store the result in comparison.
Get the adjusted R² of both (adj1, adj2).











Add cmj_depth_m to m2, then anova(m1, m2) and summary(m2)$adj.r.squared.




m1 <- lm(jump_height_m ~ con_force_rel + con_time_s, data = squad)
m2 <- lm(jump_height_m ~ con_force_rel + con_time_s + cmj_depth_m, data = squad)

comparison <- anova(m1, m2)
comparison

adj1 <- summary(m1)$adj.r.squared
adj2 <- summary(m2)$adj.r.squared
c(adj1 = adj1, adj2 = adj2)
m1 <- lm(jump_height_m ~ con_force_rel + con_time_s, data = squad)
m2 <- lm(jump_height_m ~ con_force_rel + con_time_s + cmj_depth_m, data = squad)

comparison <- anova(m1, m2)
comparison

adj1 <- summary(m1)$adj.r.squared
adj2 <- summary(m2)$adj.r.squared
c(adj1 = adj1, adj2 = adj2)












TipHow many predictors can I use?



A common rule of thumb is at least 10–20 observations per predictor. With 84 athletes, a model with 4–8 predictors is reasonable; with 20 athletes, 1–2. Too many predictors overfit: the model describes the noise of your sample and predicts new athletes badly. Choose predictors based on theory, not by trying everything (remember the multiple-comparisons problem).

title: 4.7 Multiple regression
text:
Part 4 · Multicollinearity
When predictors are strongly correlated with each other, the model struggles to separate their effects: coefficients become unstable and their standard errors inflate. Taller athletes are heavier (r = 0.84):








Adding height almost doubles the standard error of the body-mass coefficient, and its p-value goes from 0.0005 to 0.056, although body mass is just as relevant as before. Height itself adds nothing.
The variance inflation factor (VIF) quantifies this. For predictor j:
\[VIF_j = \frac{1}{1 - R^2_j}\]
where R²j comes from regressing predictor j on all the other predictors. VIF = 1 means no collinearity; VIF > 5 (some say > 10) is a warning sign. (The car package’s vif() calculates it for all predictors at once.)

Calculate the VIF of body_mass_kg in the model with height_m:

Regress body_mass_kg on height_m and get its R² (r2_j).
Calculate vif_mass.











lm(body_mass_kg ~ height_m, data = squad), then vif_mass <- 1 / (1 - r2_j).




r2_j <- summary(lm(body_mass_kg ~ height_m, data = squad))$r.squared
vif_mass <- 1 / (1 - r2_j)
vif_mass
r2_j <- summary(lm(body_mass_kg ~ height_m, data = squad))$r.squared
vif_mass <- 1 / (1 - r2_j)
vif_mass







You include both peak power and mean power (r = 0.83 with each other) as predictors of jump height. Mean power becomes non-significant. Should you conclude that mean power is unrelated to jump height?

Yes
No: mean power correlates r = 0.73 with jump height on its own; it just adds little beyond peak power, because the two predictors carry overlapping information
Yes, because peak power is more reliable


A non-significant coefficient in a multiple regression means “no unique contribution given the other predictors”, not “no relationship”.

title: 4.7 Multiple regression
text:
Checklist for multiple regression

Choose predictors from theory, and avoid predictors that are mathematically coupled to the outcome.
Plot the data first; check predictor correlations (collinearity) and VIFs.
Interpret each coefficient holding the others constant, with its 95 % CI (confint(model)).
Check residuals (plot(model) in RStudio).
Compare models with adjusted R², AIC or anova() for nested models.
Respect the sample size (10–20 observations per predictor).
Remember: adjusted associations in observational data are not proof of causation.

title: 4.9 Reliability
text:
Why reliability matters
A coach tests an athlete’s CMJ before and after a training block: 38.0 cm → 40.5 cm. Did the athlete improve? That depends on how much the result would vary anyway if nothing had changed. That’s the test’s reliability. A test with a lot of noise can’t detect small but real changes.
The trials dataset contains three CMJs of 56 professional basketball and soccer players, performed one after another in a single session. Jump height and body mass were calculated by the force-platform software for every trial:








Each athlete’s true ability didn’t change within those few minutes, so differences between trials are measurement error (biological variability + technical error).

title: 4.9 Reliability
text:
Two components of error

Systematic bias: a consistent shift between trials, e.g. athletes jump higher in trial 2 because of a warm-up or learning effect. It’s the mean of the differences.
Random error: the unpredictable trial-to-trial scatter. It’s the SD of the differences.

title: 4.9 Reliability
text:
Typical error and CV
The typical error (TE) is the standard deviation of an individual’s repeated measurements: the “± noise” of a single test result. From two trials:
\[TE = \frac{SD(\text{trial}_2 - \text{trial}_1)}{\sqrt{2}}\]
(Dividing by √2 because a difference contains the error of two measurements.) Expressed as a percentage of the mean, it’s the coefficient of variation:
\[CV = \frac{TE}{\text{mean}} \times 100\%\]

For trials 1 and 2:

Extract t1 and t2 (jump heights; trials is sorted by athlete, so they line up).
Calculate the differences d, the systematic bias (mean of d), the typical error te and the cv (use the mean of all trial 1 and 2 values).











t2 uses trial == 2; d <- t2 - t1; bias <- mean(d); te <- sd(d) / sqrt(2).




t1 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 1]
t2 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 2]

d <- t2 - t1
bias <- mean(d)
te <- sd(d) / sqrt(2)
cv <- te / mean(c(t1, t2)) * 100

round(c(bias = bias, te = te, cv = cv), 2)
t1 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 1]
t2 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 2]

d <- t2 - t1
bias <- mean(d)
te <- sd(d) / sqrt(2)
cv <- te / mean(c(t1, t2)) * 100

round(c(bias = bias, te = te, cv = cv), 2)

title: 4.9 Reliability
text:
Bland–Altman plot
A Bland–Altman plot shows agreement between two measurements: for each athlete, the difference (y) is plotted against the mean of the two trials (x). Three horizontal lines summarise it:

the bias (mean difference),
the 95 % limits of agreement: bias ± 1.96 × SD of the differences. About 95 % of differences should fall between them.

It shows whether the error depends on the size of the measurement, and it makes outliers stand out.

Complete the Bland–Altman plot of trials 1 and 2: compute ba$mean and ba$diff, the limits loa_low and loa_high, and add the three horizontal lines.










diff = t2 - t1, sd(ba$diff) in both limits, and yintercept = c(loa_low, loa_high).




t1 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 1]
t2 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 2]
ba <- data.frame(athlete = unique(trials$athlete),
                 mean = (t1 + t2) / 2,
                 diff = t2 - t1)

bias <- mean(ba$diff)
loa_low <- bias - 1.96 * sd(ba$diff)
loa_high <- bias + 1.96 * sd(ba$diff)

ggplot(ba, aes(x = mean, y = diff)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = bias) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(loa_low, loa_high), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Mean of trials 1 and 2 (cm)", y = "Trial 2 - trial 1 (cm)")
t1 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 1]
t2 <- trials$jump_height_cm[trials$trial == 2]
ba <- data.frame(athlete = unique(trials$athlete),
                 mean = (t1 + t2) / 2,
                 diff = t2 - t1)

bias <- mean(ba$diff)
loa_low <- bias - 1.96 * sd(ba$diff)
loa_high <- bias + 1.96 * sd(ba$diff)

ggplot(ba, aes(x = mean, y = diff)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = bias) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(loa_low, loa_high), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Mean of trials 1 and 2 (cm)", y = "Trial 2 - trial 1 (cm)")

title: 4.9 Reliability
text:
Finding processing errors
The force-platform software estimates body mass from the quiet-standing phase of every trial. An athlete’s mass can’t change by several kg within a few minutes, so a large difference between trials means the quiet-standing phase was not quiet (the athlete moved, or stepped on late), like CMJ 2 of Athlete K in lesson 2.5. A wrong body weight corrupts the whole force analysis, including jump height.








Athlete A02’s first trial has a body mass 2.8 kg lower than the other two, and a jump height 21 cm higher. That’s a processing error, not a jump.


Calculate the range of body mass (max − min) across each athlete’s three trials with tapply(), and store it in mass_range.
Store the IDs of the athletes with a range above 2 kg in flagged.
Recalculate the typical error of trials 1–2 without the flagged athletes (te_clean).












function(x) max(x) - min(x) (or diff(range(x)))
mass_range > 2
sd(d_clean) / sqrt(2)





# 1. Body-mass range per athlete
mass_range <- tapply(trials$body_mass_kg, trials$athlete, function(x) max(x) - min(x))

# 2. Flagged athletes
flagged <- names(mass_range)[mass_range > 2]
flagged

# 3. Typical error without the flagged athletes
clean <- subset(trials, !athlete %in% flagged)
d_clean <- clean$jump_height_cm[clean$trial == 2] - clean$jump_height_cm[clean$trial == 1]
te_clean <- sd(d_clean) / sqrt(2)
te_clean

An athlete’s estimated body mass is 82.0, 81.8 and 76.4 kg in three consecutive jumps. What do you do with trial 3?

Keep it: biological variation is normal
Treat it as suspect: the quiet-standing phase was probably disturbed, so its body weight, and therefore its jump height, is unreliable; re-analyse it or exclude it
Average the three body masses and keep all jump heights


A 5-kg change in a minute is impossible. Because body weight is used to calculate acceleration, velocity and jump height, an error in it propagates to everything.

title: 4.9 Reliability
text:
Relative reliability: the ICC
The TE describes absolute reliability (in cm). The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) describes relative reliability: how well the test keeps athletes in the same rank order across trials. It compares the variability between athletes with the error within athletes (0 = no reliability, 1 = perfect).
You can calculate it from an ANOVA with athlete and trial as factors. One common form, ICC(3,1) (consistency of single measurements), is:
\[ICC = \frac{MS_{athletes} - MS_{error}}{MS_{athletes} + (k - 1)\, MS_{error}}\]
where k is the number of trials.








Common benchmarks (Koo & Li, 2016): < 0.5 poor, 0.5–0.75 moderate, 0.75–0.9 good, > 0.9 excellent. Cleaning the data moves the ICC from “moderate” to “good”. (The irr and psych packages calculate all ICC forms with confidence intervals.)






WarningA high ICC can hide a large error



The ICC depends on how different the athletes are. In a very heterogeneous group (youth players and professionals together), the ICC can be excellent even if the TE is large. Always report the TE or CV as well.

title: 4.9 Reliability
text:
The smallest worthwhile change
How big must a change be to matter? For team-sport athletes, a common approach defines the smallest worthwhile change (SWC) as 0.2 × the between-athlete SD, i.e. a “small” effect size (Hopkins).
Compare the TE with the SWC:

TE < SWC: the test can detect the smallest worthwhile change in a single athlete (“good” sensitivity),
TE ≈ SWC: “OK”, averaging several trials helps,
TE > SWC: the test is too noisy to detect the SWC in individuals.


Using the cleaned data:

Calculate the between-athlete SD of trial 1 jump heights and the swc.
Calculate te_clean again (trials 1–2) and the ratio te_clean / swc.
Calculate the typical error of the mean of 3 trials, te_mean3, using the CLT: TE / √3.











swc <- 0.2 * sd(c1), ratio <- te_clean / swc, te_mean3 <- te_clean / sqrt(3).




mass_range <- tapply(trials$body_mass_kg, trials$athlete, function(x) max(x) - min(x))
clean <- subset(trials, !athlete %in% names(mass_range)[mass_range > 2])
c1 <- clean$jump_height_cm[clean$trial == 1]
c2 <- clean$jump_height_cm[clean$trial == 2]

# 1. Smallest worthwhile change
swc <- 0.2 * sd(c1)

# 2. Typical error and ratio
te_clean <- sd(c2 - c1) / sqrt(2)
ratio <- te_clean / swc

# 3. Typical error of the mean of 3 trials
te_mean3 <- te_clean / sqrt(3)

round(c(swc = swc, te = te_clean, ratio = ratio, te_mean3 = te_mean3), 2)
mass_range <- tapply(trials$body_mass_kg, trials$athlete, function(x) max(x) - min(x))
clean <- subset(trials, !athlete %in% names(mass_range)[mass_range > 2])
c1 <- clean$jump_height_cm[clean$trial == 1]
c2 <- clean$jump_height_cm[clean$trial == 2]

# 1. Smallest worthwhile change
swc <- 0.2 * sd(c1)

# 2. Typical error and ratio
te_clean <- sd(c2 - c1) / sqrt(2)
ratio <- te_clean / swc

# 3. Typical error of the mean of 3 trials
te_mean3 <- te_clean / sqrt(3)

round(c(swc = swc, te = te_clean, ratio = ratio, te_mean3 = te_mean3), 2)







CMJ: TE = 1.5 cm, SWC = 1.0 cm. An athlete improves from 41.0 to 42.0 cm. What’s the best conclusion?

The athlete improved by a worthwhile amount
The change equals the SWC but is smaller than the noise of the test; it may well be measurement error
The test is useless


A 1 cm change is well within ±1.5 cm (one TE) of random variation. You’d need a larger change, or repeated tests, to be confident.



Why does averaging three trials reduce the typical error by a factor of √3?

Because the best trial is always the most accurate
Because random errors partly cancel out; by the central limit theorem, the SD of a mean of n values is SD/√n
It doesn’t: averaging only removes systematic bias


Exactly the standard-error logic of lesson 2.4. It assumes the errors of the trials are independent.

title: 4.9 Reliability
text:
Lesson summary

Bias = mean of the trial differences; TE = SD(differences) / √2; CV = TE / mean × 100.
Bland–Altman: difference vs. mean, with bias ± 1.96 SD limits of agreement.
ICC: relative reliability from an ANOVA; always report it together with the TE/CV.
SWC = 0.2 × between-athlete SD; a test is sensitive when TE ≤ SWC. Averaging n trials divides TE by √n.
Check data quality (e.g. body-mass consistency): a few processing errors can make a good test look bad.
